If you have any suspicion, please confirm with the sender verbally that this email is authentic. If you suspect fraud, click "Phish Alert Report."

Good afternoon Stephanie,
Pursuant to our conversation this afternoon UCSD would like to formalize a request for a minor scope amendment to reflect the change in focus and technical content of the Regional Water Equity Report convening slated for Wednesday, April 26th.  As the focus of the meeting will no longer be based on the contents of the drought impact literature review being conducted by UCSD, and as the need for and focus of presentation content and public information has changed, we would like to request approval of the following:

1. UCSD will focus on completion of a technical presentation highlighting preliminary findings of the literature review, submitted in powerpoint format by Friday, April 14th for editing and translation.  It is our understanding that the length of the presentation may be anywhere from ten minutes to roughly one hour, depending on the County’s selection of additional presenters with technical content.

2.  UCSD will complete a summary of the technical presentation for the public meeting.  This will be a graphic-rich handout in print and web-compatible format (likely powerpoint) by Friday, April 14th, offering key information and links in a form suitable for the general public and with links for further information to technical sources.

3.  For the meeting itself, UCSD will NOT be responsible for agendas, printing, name tags, etc.  as it is our understanding that Murakawa Communications has been contracted to supply these materials.  UCSD will have roughly ten (10) students present to assist with sign-in, logistics, polling, and collecting public comments.  UCSD’s students will have (10) iPads with them, with connectivity suitable for use for PollEverywhere questions for those without devices.

3.  UCSD will resume work on the literature review after the meeting, adding a review of available water rate information for San Diego and Imperial Counties and the bi-national region.  The meeting summary likewise will be completed.

Thank you Stephanie for your support and leadership!
Sincerely,
JB

Subject: [External] RWER Task 3.B - Facilities Inventory and Screening Submittal

Hi Stephanie,

The Task 3.B deliverable is on Sharepoint in the Task 3.B folder <https://projectsitesb.geosyntec.com/8/SW033129-0547/_layouts/15/start.aspx#/SitePages/Home.aspx?RootFolder=%2F8%2FSW033129-0547%2FShared%20Documents%2FTask%203%20-%20SW%20Capture%20and%20Use%20at%20County%20Parks%20and%20Facilities%2FTask%203B%20Deliverable&FolderCTID=0x012000BB8DC2F928EF0944BBEB156EFA200989&View=%7B09ED6256-943F-4252-81B3-27AB4979A7B9%7D> . As discussed on the call today, the table presents the attributes associated with each County facility, supporting the potential infiltration and diversion screening as well as the next Task 3.C's prioritization and identification of potential project opportunities. These facilities are compiled from the Task 3.A deliverable and include the additional facilities you sent on 7/3 from the missing data we identified during that task. The following two tabs are included for the Task 3.B deliverable:

*	Attributes, Rationale, and Desc: This tab provides the rationale, sources, and description of the various attributes added to each facility.
*	FAC_INF_DIV_CAP_RESULTS: This tab provides the attribute results for each facility, along with the infiltration and diversion screening results. The initial screening criteria for feasible infiltration and diversion for water supply in Columns O and P are listed below. Onsite Capture and Use screening will be shown during Task 3.C. Additionally, we have included if the parcel overlaps with a SWCFS Parcel, has dry weather flows at MS4 outfalls within 500ft sourced from WSP, and has water demands based on the data provided by the County in May.

Task 3.C will identify the potential project opportunities based on additional applied criteria to rule out areas not ideal for infiltration, diversion, or onsite capture and use (e.g., not within 40ft of septic parcels or 100ft of contamination sites, already has recycled water etc.). and include the weights and resulting scores for each of the facilities along with the prioritized list based on the prioritization framework.

It would be helpful to know if you would like us to remove leased facilities or if there are any other facilities we should remove prior to the prioritization and identification of potential project opportunities. Additionally, let us know if you would like us to include any other attributes for these facilities to support Task 3.C. Please provide this information by July 21 if possible.

1.	Infiltration

	a.	Infiltration screening

		*	Groundwater basins within 1-mile buffer, or;
		*	Within 1-Mile of a drinking well, but outside 150 feet of a drinking well, and;
		*	Permeable geology (Alluvium, Basalt, Conglomerate, Sandstone), and;
		*	Slopes <15%.

2.	Diversion

	a.	Diversion screening

		*	Within sewershed to recycled water treatment plant

Please let us know if you have questions!

Thank you!

Subject: San Diego County Regional Water Equity Report (RWER)

Good afternoon Mr. Roy,

Thank you for your time this morning. I am following up with information about the Regional Water Equity Assessment/Report. As I mentioned to you over the phone, we are at the tail end of stakeholder interviews and would love to get your interview included in our report by the 31st of May. I have attached a fact sheet on the project and the interview questions that we would like to ask you with our GeoSyntec consultants if you are able to participate. I have cc’d Elise Ruiz who is the lead of this project in the Office of Sustainability and Environmental Justice.

Essentially, this process of assessing what communities are/are not able to do to reach water equity in terms of sustainability through stormwater capturing, wastewater systems, and greywater strategies will provide a report to the County Board of Supervisors this September. We see this report being a reference to future policy and potential funding.

I saw that you accepted the calendar invite for Thursday the 25th at 2:00 p.m. to meet with Elise and me. If you find that you might be available to do the interview then, we could a lot more time and check with GeoSyntecs availability.

Hi Stephanie,
The contract years for both contracts end on May 31st. New capacity is available June 1st.

For either contract, it may be possible to “partially encumber” funding for a new task order prior to the end of the contract year, and then encumber the rest of the funds needed in the new contract year. Something similar was done for the green streets master plan task order. I’m not sure if this is common practice, or if it could be done as easily with a PER.

This would require coordination with Danielle. When this was been done before, we waited until the very end of the contract year to encumber funds and use up remaining capacity. Something to discuss.

-Chris

Hi Joel,

Thanks again for your participation in the interview for this project.  We do have a couple follow up questions we’d like your input on below.  These are not meant to take more than 10-15 minutes of your time and it would greatly benefit our analysis.  Also, when able, we’d definitely be interested in viewing the maps you mentioned showing historic and current extents of agriculture, as well as ideal lands to increase agriculture throughout the region.

	a.	What do you see as the biggest risk(s) to the San Diego and Imperial region’s water supply portfolio with respect to long-term resilience?

Cost - heavy regional infrastructure investment creates a burden on consumers that they may not be able to support for uses that do not benefit them. Solutions need to be localized to individual communities to ensure resident buy-in and ability to pay. Communities need to be engaged to create community-specific drought resilience plans to prepare for reduced allocations at a neighborhood-level during drought conditions. To ease this burden, non-essential irrigation and consumptions should be eliminated and/or disincentivized with a heavily graduated pay scale based on per-capita volume for residential and commercial customers. This will incentivize further conservation, allowing for existing water supplies to be allocated more equitably. As an essential service for local residents, agricultural allocations should receive priority up to 1/3 of the regional allocation at special rates, so long as these farms contribute to the local food supply. We must prioritize use of precious water resources for urban greening in low-income neighborhoods and for agricultural production for local consumption in order to ensure regional resilience during drought conditions.

	a.	Can you identify the top three water management projects types/solutions that you’d recommend the San Diego and Imperial region allocate more funding/effort towards?

                                                         i.      Regional Water Recycling

                                                       ii.      Localized On-Site Reuse (Graywater) - First, see below.

                                                     iii.      Stormwater Capture and Reuse/Recycling

                                                     iv.      Desalination - Third; costly but reliable source during drought conditions depending on energy availability

                                                       v.      Storage Management - Increase Dam Capacity

                                                     vi.      Storage Management - Manage Groundwater Recharge

                                                   vii.      Conservation - Second; eliminate non-essential consumption to alleviate water budget.

	a.	Which of the following water supply solutions do you view at the “most at risk” in terms of being a reliable, long term source of water for the region? Which is “least at risk”?  Write “most risk” and “least risk” after two of the options below, and elaborate in 1-2 sentences on why.

                                                         i.      Regional Water Recycling

                                                       ii.      Localized On-Site Reuse (Graywater) - Least Risk

                                                     iii.      Stormwater Capture and Reuse/Recycling

                                                     iv.      Desalination

                                                       v.      Storage Management - Increase Dam Capacity

                                                     vi.      Storage Management - Manage Groundwater Recharge - Most Risk

                                                   vii.      Conservation

Least risk - Graywater use effectively eliminates the need for landscape irrigation, which is responsible for roughly half of urban water consumption. This is one of the most effective forms of conservation with the most co-benefits. In terms of resilience, localized systems such as graywater application are more effective at using water with less maintenance costs than largescale regional infrastructure.

Greatest risk - extraction from groundwater basins must be monitored and regulated based on recharge rates in order to avoid depletion. For this reason, groundwater basins are not currently relied upon for urban areas. However, aquifer levels should be monitored and managed in areas which are adding new residential developments, ex: San Pasqual Valley.

Thank you,

Stephanie

Hi Joel,

We met at the San Diego Water Assembly last week (4/26) and I wanted to follow up with you.  Our team is working with the County of San Diego’s Office of Sustainability and Environmental Justice (OSEJ) on identifying drought resilience approaches for San Diego and Imperial Counties as well as border communities in Mexico.  We would like to request a 1-hour virtual interview which will include questions around sustainable and equitable drought management practices and solutions throughout this region.  If you are open to this, please let us know and Chrissie (cc’d) will follow up with you on scheduling.

For some additional background, in September 2022, the County of San Diego Board of Supervisors directed staff to take a proactive, regional approach to address the drought crisis through drought management and water sustainability practices. Our team is leading up the research and recommendations related to various solutions including water recycling, desalination, conservation, storage systems and stormwater capture through the lens of equity. We are currently working with local partners to identify promising ideas and key needs.

Hope to speak with you soon.

subject: Water Equity Project
body:
Good afternoon, Sam,

I want to introduce you to Elise Ruiz, our Group Program Manager in OSEJ. Elise is working on a big Water Equity Project directed by the Board of Supervisors, and I thought it would be great for the two of you to connect and discuss potential outreach opportunities and collaboration.

The project is focused on an assessment of water equity and sustainability through stormwater capturing in our diverse communities. I am assisting with tribal outreach, but I thought you might have connections with CBOs that could benefit from joining this initiative. To me, racial inequity leads us to conversations about water, housing, infrastructure, health, and environmental injustice. Elise is highly focused on engagement from all communities in the region.

Attached is brief fact sheet about the project but Elise could provide you more information about her goals for outreach and outcomes. Elise, if you would like me to participate in this conversation, please feel free to include me on the invite. ??

Thank you and have a lovely week,

Roberta Leash (She/Her/Hers)

subject: RE: Research/Response on Stormwater Capture/Use
body:
One more nugget of info, from the study:

"Title 22 of California's Water Recycling Criteria refers to California state guidelines for how treated and recycled water is discharged and used. The standards also require the state's Department of Health Services to develop and enforce water and bacteriological treatment standards for water recycling and reuse. However, whether or not Title 22 would apply to irrigation projects is unclear at this time."

Best,

Stephanie Gaines

PM, DPW WPP

619-964-8337

From: Gaines, Stephanie
Sent: Wednesday, May 31, 2023 2:21 PM
To: Lawrance, Christopher <Christopher.Lawrance@sdcounty.ca.gov>
Subject: Research/Response on Stormwater Capture/Use

Hi Chris - I have another request, which I hope will be a quick one.

Another consulting firm is gathering data for the Regional Water Equity Report (RWER), this time the Affordable Housing component. One question is related to regulations and requirements around capturing and using stormwater "indoors and outdoors". Our rain barrel, and onsite collection efforts from roof runoff (think cisterns, or larger scale capture from onsite runoff and rooftops for landscapes) are legally allowed; large scale offsite harvesting for larger scale use, are not always. some are subject to Title 22 regulations, or the new SB966 regs you've been watching the state's website for. Additionally, we (County and City, and likely other jurisdictions) don't have regulations related to stormwater (that I'm aware of!) Can you respond to their question below and develop a response that focuses on local stormwater capture/use by tomorrow morning?

Just a note; our SWCFS tech memos do have some language on regulations, primarily related to "regulatory ambiguity", meaning we don't' have clear or specific requirements for stormwater use. We know treatment for larger scale (think parks, golf courses) above ground irrigation use must meet Title 22 requirements.

1.	What are the County water quality (i.e., treatment) requirements for using rainwater outdoors / indoors? We're unable to locate standards in either the County or City of San Diego codes.

Best,

Hi Marcus,

Thanks again for volunteering to participate in a one-hour (virtual) interview with LDC staff, LDC’s sub-consultant (ARUP), and County staff.  Below is a list of meeting times for your consideration.  Our goal is to meet asap with your organization.  Please identify all times that may work for you. I’ve cc’d the folks you listed in your email below.  If necessary, I will send additional dates/times if none of these options work for your team.  I will circulate an agenda and send out a Teams meeting invite as soon as a meeting time has been identified.

*	Friday, June 9th at 4 PM
*	Tuesday, June 13th at 11 AM
*	Tuesday, June 13th at 4 PM
*	Tuesday, June 13th at 3 PM [Please note: this time is not preferred as there is currently a schedule conflict with County of San Diego staff]

Below is a preliminary list of questions that we are anticipating to ask during the interview.  These questions will help to guide our meeting.

*	We are exploring several water conservation, greywater reuse and stormwater reuse strategies for new and rehabilitation affordable housing projects in San Diego County. Have you implemented any of these strategies before?

	*	If so, what did you implement and how did you pay for it/them (e.g., programs, incentives, loans, tax credits etc.)?

	*	How effective were the measures (e.g., water savings, payback, operational performance successes/challenges)?

	*	What would you implement again? If not, why not?

	*	Is there more (efficiency / reuse measures) you would have done if more funding was available?

	*	Please describe, if applicable, how your organization has utilized LEED certification for different development types to help achieve water conservation, greywater reuse, and/or stormwater strategies for affordable housing projects. Do you have LEED accredited staff?

	*	Do you have year over year data on the projects’ water/sewer expenses before and after water conservation measures were implemented (if applicable)? If so, could you please share that data with us?

Subject: [EXTERNAL] San Diego Regional Water Equity Report Follow-up

**This email came from an external source. Be cautious about clicking on any links in this email or opening attachments.**
________________________________

Hi Julie,

Thank you for your participation in the San Diego Regional Water Equity Project interview.  We greatly appreciate your time and all the helpful input you provided.  As discussed, we do have a couple follow up items we’d like to request from you below.  If we could get responses within the next 2 weeks, it would be much appreciated. (Keli – we hope you feel better soon!)

  1.  CIP Equity Scoring Sheets – you mentioned a “scoring sheet” that is now a component of prioritizing and selecting CIP projects.  If public, can you share an example with us?  If not public, we’d be interested to understand how you incorporate equity into your project selection.  We will be doing a similar exercise on a larger scale as part of this project, so are very interested in your methodology.  If not public, perhaps a 30 minute phone call over the next month or two would be very much appreciated.

The scoring sheets themselves are not public (and likely not entirely useful), but here is the link to the council policy that guided the new approach to include equity as a condition for prioritization (https://docs.sandiego.gov/councilpolicies/cpd_800-14.pdf). PUD further defined a couple factors to inform our scoring that considers project location, economic development in structurally excluded communities, economic growth in communities of concern, and public impact. Happy to participate in a phone call if you’d like to discuss methodology more.

  1.  Reservoir Storage Capacities - Are the reservoir storage capacities provided under this link Reservoir Lakes | City of San Diego Official Website<https://www.sandiego.gov/reservoirs-lakes> considering current dam restrictions? If not, could you provide the maximum height storage capacities instead?

They do not and yes I can. The reservoirs with height restrictions include El Capitan, Hodges, and Morena (self-imposed restriction). The allowable storage capacity with height restrictions are ~50,000 AF, 5,999 AF, and 16,742 AF, respectively.

  1.  Pure Water Clarification - For Pure Water Phase 1, we understand the North City Water Reclamation Plant (52 MGD recycled water) is being expanded to provide flow to the North City Pure Water Facility (30 MGD of purified water). What portion of the recycled water flow (if any) is being provided to existing recycled water customers once Pure Water is online?

The City will be honoring existing agreements with recycled water customers. The City is in the process of reviewing our recycled water policy to ensure it aligns with Pure Water needs.

  1.  Recycled Water Sewersheds and Service Areas – As we assess potential regional diversion and capture and use opportunities, we would like to map the sewersheds and service areas to/from the City’s recycled water facilities, including Pure Water. Would it be possible to put us in touch with someone to help with that request? Ideally, we are looking for GIS shapefiles beyond those available on SANGIS.

 Huy Nguyen (HTNguyen@sandiego.gov<mailto:HTNguyen@sandiego.gov>), Senior Engineer. Some data may be considered protected for security reasons. Specific requests will be evaluated once received.

  1.  Interview Follow-up Questions – as discussed, we would also like your input on the questions below.  Please let me know if you need clarification on any of them:

     *   What do you see as the biggest risk(s) to the region’s water supply portfolio with respect to long-term resilience?

While we are excited that Pure Water San Diego will be supplying nearly half of our water supply, we must not get complacent about our continued reliance on imported water. There is always risk associated with imported supplies that include influence by drought/disaster. We are partnering with San Diego County Water Authority on their Master Plan and will continue our own strategic Long Range Water Resource Planning that goes beyond Pure Water SD.

     *   How would you recommend that the San Diego Region allocate future efforts/resources toward the following water supply solutions, by percentage:

                                                               i.      Regional Water Recycling

                                                             ii.      Localized On-Site Reuse (e.g. Graywater)

                                                           iii.      Stormwater Capture and Reuse/Recycling

                                                           iv.      Desalination

                                                             v.      Storage Management - Reservoir Storage and Dam Management

                                                           vi.      Storage Management - Manage Groundwater Recharge

                                                          vii.      Conservation

Not sure I could put a percentage to any of these strategies, they all play such a critical role. I would say that while conservation is still valuable and our education must continue, I’ll echo statements made by Governor Newsom that we cannot conserve our way out of drought. The low-hanging fruit for conservation has mostly been achieved. Our indoor use rates are already practically aligned with very aggressive State targets and will not likely get much lower (and as we discussed during our meeting, lower indoor use could reduce the flows needed to operate Pure Water SD). We still must target outdoor water use, but the best way forward to address issues of supply is to get more creative about our storage solutions and investigate feasibility of other supply sources. I’ll also note that localized on-site reuse, while supported by the City with a permitting process, is not something the City actively promotes because of our regional water recycling program. Localized on-site reuse is better suited for communities that do not have a regional program.

     *   Which of the following water supply solutions do you view at the “most at risk” in terms of being a reliable, long term source of water for the region? Which is “least at risk”?  Write “most risk” and “least risk” after two of the options below, and elaborate in 1-2 sentences on why.

                                                               i.      Regional Water Recycling

                                                             ii.      Localized On-Site Reuse (Graywater)

                                                           iii.      Stormwater Capture and Reuse/Recycling – Most Risk

                                                           iv.      Desalination

                                                             v.      Storage Management – Reservoir Storage and Dam Management – Least Risk

                                                           vi.      Storage Management - Managed Groundwater Recharge

Any strategy that relies on rainwater will be considered “most risky” due to the fact that we know we will be seeing longer dry periods punctuated by heavy storms, and those dry periods would create burdens to water suppliers needing to provide a consistent year-round supply. The better way to make use of those heavy storms, and the option with “least risk”, is leaning into our storage management, particularly in the realm of reservoir storage and dam management.

Thanks again for all your assistance in support of this project.

Stephanie

Sarah-

My team met with the group described below on Friday (UCSD, SANDAG, Climate Action Campaign was added & UCSD spoke with the City of SD earlier so they did not join).  UCSD is looking for us to sign onto a Letter of Intent by COB today including providing bios and resumes of key staff.  The LOI is a precursor to be able to apply for the grant.   In short, there is much to be flushed out with this research effort before committing to join a grant application.  We don't think there is application to the CAP but there may be for the Sustainable Land Use Framework, possibly RDF and other data analyses that the PODS could lead.  It is not clear if the ROI would be there for us.  This type of thing can easily balloon into a substantial work effort, which we would not be able to commit to with our current project responsibilities.  However, the City plans to join (I believe SANDAG does, too, but confirming) and we think it would be better to sign on than miss the opportunity, recognizing that the LOI is an initial formality and we can drop off prior to grant application if we determine the ROI doesn't pencil.  We were very transparent with the group that it sounds like there are exciting possibilities here but we cannot commit until we know more.

Question by COB: Are you ok with us moving forward at this preliminary stage, recognizing we will need to flush out more details and reassess prior to joining on any formal application? (We can also give the BOS offices a heads up asap, if so.)

More detail about the grant project

*	Goal: Create a tool that uses existing data to help support decision-making

	*	Scenario planning tool
	*	Performance based approach
	*	Seeks to fill existing gaps in data analysis and layering (looking at the intersection of various existing data, etc.)
	*	To be designed based on what our needs are (i.e., parking policies, SB-9, relationship between built and natural environment to things like ghg, health and other impacts)
	*	(Not applicable to CAP because there are prescribed or highly vetted methodologies for the CAP work and new tools are not needed)

*	2 years up to $10M (likely 2-5M more than enough)
*	Outcomes- critical that the tool is used and the outcomes are the crux of the project

Ask/ County Obligation:

*	In-kind match- UCSD indicated this would not be a monetary match from us- no funding; some resources may even pass through UCSD and support our activities
*	Help shape proposal- collect data we have, participate in interactive working groups (outreach, other agencies)
*	Commit to ongoing use of research
*	Looking for suburban land use authority (other jurisdiction)

UCSD is requesting bios and resume for the County's representatives by COB today.  We propose myself, Rami (for now- possibly swap with new PODs Deputy in the future), Murtaza, Don Chase (LRP Planning Manager).

Thank you.

Dahvia

Subject: [External] Climate Action Research Grant - Letter of Intent (LOI) Due Jan 17th
Importance: High

Hi Everyone:

I hope you are all doing well and had a wonderful holiday season!  I am writing to provide an overview of the Climate Action Research Grant Program and the formation of a San Diego based team, and next steps.

Climate Action Research Grant Program

Just before the holidays in December, the state of California finally released the long awaited call for research (and action) proposals for projects that can demonstrate the ability to hit the ground running and sustain lasting practical and GHG mitigation, reduction and  impacts.  These will be 2 year projects ranging from around 500k up to $10 Million.  A letter of intent (LOI)  is due January 17th which is very soon for projects both with or without matching funds.

We are fortunate to have received a great deal of enthusiasm from all of the partners needed to generate a very competitive application.  The City of San Diego, San Diego County, SANDAG, the Climate Action Campaign, UCSD and other research partners have the ability to form a very strong team with complementary roles and skills that meet the requirements of this RFP.  Each organization has expressed an interest in working together to leverage our collective strengths, expertise, resources, and interests to create a strong and competitive LOI.  It is also possible that we may have the ability to show a significant matching funds by directly supporting other synergistic efforts underway in our region.  Foremost, I will soon be introducing the researchers who will be part of this effort - drawn from several research institutions.

We all share a collective interest and vision for reducing travel and place-based GHG emissions, providing affordable housing, and promoting public health, social justice, and safety through transit and active transportation investments combined with sustainable land use practices.  The policy and regulatory environment is rapidly changing with significant advancements at the state, regional, and local level taking place.  The immediate goal is to craft a compelling LOI that is sufficiently focused and targeted while also being general enough to be something we can all agree to quickly to get the green light from the state to move on to the proposal development stage where we will truly craft our work plan and what we want to accomplish.  There is a tremendous amount of work underway within each of our member organizations to generate a very unique and compelling project.

Next Steps

1.	Confirming who is on our team
2.	Getting your input - convening to discuss focus for LOI - stay tuned
3.	Drafting the AIMS, objectives, approach, and products
4.	Creating budget, timeline, and confirming match
5.	Completing letters of support
6.	Meeting all LOI requirements (see below)
7.	Filing LOI by the 17th

RFP Overview

The RFP can be found at this link: 2023 Request for Proposals (RFP) for the California Climate Action Research Initiative <https://urldefense.com/v3/__https:/ucop.us12.list-manage.com/track/click?u=2ae4678f6e94927e764ad58e5&id=2b1d6c9087&e=bdebfa5d99__;!!Mih3wA!C1EvLsrcFiLia4KrfJdlY70QxN39F1ZYvogi7XN4zYQMjSavP3C5PmbMvgHyowNMdVAe1s49NEnRFlYxhkb3QKU$> .  "The CA Climate Action Research Grants are intended to spur innovative applied research that addresses California's climate goals, ensures that local communities are prepared and resilient, and prevents future disasters. This Request for Proposals (RFP) outlines two grant categories: CA Climate Action Seed Grants and CA Climate Action Matching Grants. Proposals for both grant categories must be synergistic with the State of California's climate action priority or priorities. The California Climate Adaptation Strategy, in particular, presents a holistic vision for the state with the following outcome- based priorities:

1.	Strengthen protections for climate vulnerable communities
2.	Bolster public health and safety to protect against increasing climate risks
3.	Build a climate resilient economy
4.	Accelerate nature-based climate solutions and strengthen climate resilience of natural systems
5.	Make decisions based on the best available climate science
6.	Partner and collaborate to leverage resources

There are several goals and actions under each priority area. Together, this set of priorities requires the participation of multiple disciplines and different types of partners. There are also many other state resources and strategic plans that highlight agency-specific priorities. Appendix A provides a partial list of these resources.  An important emphasis of both grant programs is near-term outcome-based solutions for public impact. (See Sec. 2.4.) To that end, proposal teams must consider thoughtful partnerships, broadly defined based on the proposed project, that will lead to high-impact solutions informed by collective insights and experiences.

Letter of Intent

A letter of intent (LOI) is required for both grant categories. The Applicant PI must specify whether they are applying for a Seed Grant or Matching Grant. Then they must complete the appropriate application materials in the RGPO SmartSimple portal.

Letter of Intent Content. LOI submissions must include the following information:

*	Proposal title (100 characters or less)
*	Identification of Applicant PI and three-page biosketch/CV upload
*	Identification of Co-PIs, Co-Investigators/senior personnel, and other participating personnel

and/or organizations, institutions, or agencies, and a three-page biosketch/CV for each
o IdentifyatleastoneotherCaliforniaacademic/researchinstitutioncollaborator(requiredfor

Matching Grant; encouraged for Seed Grant).
o Identify at least one community/end-user partner (required for Matching Grant; encouraged for

Seed Grant). See Appendix B.

*	Specific California climate priority or priorities the research will address, with links to supporting

agency documents or reports (required). See Appendix A.

*	Actionable outcome(s) expected from the project
*	Abstract/Project Summary addressing the proposed scope of research and activities, rationale, and

potential impact and expected outcomes (2400 characters max)

*	Brief plans for required programmatic components, including collaboration plan, plan for engaging

communities and other end-users, and approach to leveraging available climate related resources,

or infrastructure.

*	Keywords: Research Categories and Identifiers to be selected from a drop-down menu.
*	Seed Grants only: Specific plan for leveraging the Seed Grant during or immediately after grant

period (specific grant or other funding source or opportunity)

*	Matching Grants only: Anticipated contributions for matching commitments (cash and/or in-kind).

See Appendix C.

Dr. Lawrence Frank, Professor

                                                               i.      the items on green industry that Sarah shared was not included in Chairwoman's talking points

Cc: Lawson, Jennifer <Jennifer.Lawson@sdcounty.ca.gov<mailto:Jennifer.Lawson@sdcounty.ca.gov>>; Boghossian Ambrose, Nicole <Nicole.Ambrose@sdcounty.ca.gov<mailto:Nicole.Ambrose@sdcounty.ca.gov>>; Rasoulzadeh, Yasamin <Yasamin.Rasoulzadeh@sdcounty.ca.gov<mailto:Yasamin.Rasoulzadeh@sdcounty.ca.gov>>; De La Rosa, Michael <Michael.DeLaRosa@sdcounty.ca.gov<mailto:Michael.DeLaRosa@sdcounty.ca.gov>>
Subject: RE: OSEJ/RDF Steering Committee Agenda

Hi Murtaza and all -  great meeting on Friday and we received a lot of DCAO input and direction. I added the main action items below, based on Sarah’s feedback.

  1.  Regional Decarbonization Framework
     *   DCAO: we need to foster the business community as well as workforce. Wherever we talk about green jobs we need to talk about green industry. They go hand in hand.
                                                               i.      Murtaza need to follow up with David Flores - the items on green industry that Sarah shared was not included in Chairwoman's talking points
                                                             ii.      We need to highlight both -- it is not one or the other -- Sarah needs help reinforcing this piece with D1 (or else we will face obstacles in the business community.

     *   DCAO feedback on Symposium: Donna needs to be engaged on this -- she needs to take the lead on this. Sarah requests a meeting (30 min) to talk about the symposium
                                                               i.      We need to come back with Sarah on our plan to move forward, then have another call with David and other partners

     *   DCAO feedback on D3 convening: need to put a timeframe of when the convening needs to take place. If she can't make it then we need to move forward on it. Hold them to a timeline (because we need it for the BL, Board hearing, etc.). Can't have their district missing in this.
     *   DCAO question for us to consider: Because we are bringing this home through public health -- for purposes of when we go to the Board - should we tee up some joint Public Health approach/PPT for March hearing?
     *   DCAO: how many Playbook copies are we printing? Maybe print one for each Board office and our office -- like 30 or 40
     *   DCAO: Sarah wants information as the comments come in on the Playbook -- we may not include things proactively -- but have them discuss in the public setting
  1.  Regional Equity Group
     *   For when Murakawa meets with Sarah: how do we ensure all of our communities are represented? Not just cities, but unincorporated as well. Who will they engage? Who are the players for the
                                                               i.      What info do we need to provide them so they are educated about San Diego region dynamics -- this will be important
                                                             ii.      Connect Murakawa with PDS EJ team

  1.  Regional Water Equity Project
     *   DCAO: always Board office that moves a Board letter forward - they should be in the know. But also the whole Board took action. Start with key Board office, and then say that we are going to share with all office because we need to meet the needs. Different Board offices will have different perspectives of this -- like all the ag and Borrego Springs (worst groundwater impacted in the State) -- they have critical needs.
                                                               i.      For the one pager -- who needs to weigh in, in additional to the Board offices -- Donna, Michael. Need people far removed to review and provide insight

     *   DCAO: would like a timeline on all aspects of outreach, when will we start to make the pitch - before it starts
  1.  Misc.
     *   DCAO briefing request: would like a briefing on Spring Valley communities in terms of what we are doing for TCC grant.
                                                               i.      How are PDS and DPW involved in these conversations
                                                             ii.      As we are moving forward on SLTF -- what is the alignment, what is the overlap
                                                           iii.      Anything related to road planning, housing planning
                                                           iv.      How are we pulling this all together globally
                                                             v.      How is the work we are doing as part of TCC -- into the parcel by parcel analysis and SLUF

subject: RE: Standing Meeting Acton Items
body:
Hi Stephanie,

I’m glad you tracked down the Board Letter regarding the Water Equity recommendation. Also if you and your team are interested, this is the recording of the Board Meeting introducing the Action (Item 6) for the September hearing: Board of Supervisors Meeting (granicus.com)<https://sdcounty.granicus.com/player/clip/3312?view_id=9&redirect=true&h=2e5f6845f5743deede7d05eddca8ef95>

I’ve added some of my status updates to your notes below. I’ll follow up with you early next week with more.

Thanks for the great progress so far and have a great weekend!
Elise

From: Stephanie Zinn <Stephanie.Zinn@Geosyntec.com>
Sent: Thursday, January 19, 2023 3:33 PM
To: Ruiz, Elise <Elise.Ruiz@sdcounty.ca.gov>
Cc: Megan Otto <MMOtto@Geosyntec.com>
Subject: [External] Standing Meeting Acton Items

Hi Elise,

Thanks for the great call today.  I’ll be uploading the meeting notes to the Sharepoint site so all can see main discussion points.  Also, we were able to locate that Board Letter so I will be reviewing it this week to help better understand the history.  In the meantime, please see below for action items:

County

  *   Communication protocol for DEHQ & PDS + departmental contacts (for graywater / stormwater capture interviews) I’ve been in touch with department directors and waiting for responses - will have more for you early next week.
  *   Provide thoughts on Military / Tribes /Water Agency stakeholders to interview + preferred cities/entities for bi-national interviews (Mexicali and Tijuana over Valle de Guadalupe) I’ve met with our internal outreach team and got more direction with tribal and binational contacts. I will brief you on these updates during our next meeting. I have one contact for military and am in the process of doing more research.
  *   Confirmation that it is acceptable to interview stakeholders outside of California (e.g. Arizona graywater practices) I spoke with Murtaza and he advises that as long as this is for research/exploratory purposes based on the subject matter it is ok to contact outside of the San Diego region.

Geosyntec

  *   Provide draft interview list early next week (~1/23)
  *   Send invite for 30 minute standing meeting (best option appears to be Wednesday 1-130)
  *   Send the following:
     *   UCSD referenced studies + their dates
     *   Chula Vista Healthier Cities link
     *   List of potential elected officials
     *   List of Labor/Workforce recommended stakeholders specifically for Murtaza review

Please let me know if I missed anything.

Thank you,
Stephanie

Hi Joel,

We met at the San Diego Water Assembly last week (4/26) and I wanted to follow up with you.  Our team is working with the County of San Diego’s Office of Sustainability and Environmental Justice (OSEJ) on identifying drought resilience approaches for San Diego and Imperial Counties as well as border communities in Mexico.  We would like to request a 1-hour virtual interview which will include questions around sustainable and equitable drought management practices and solutions throughout this region.  If you are open to this, please let us know and Chrissie (cc’d) will follow up with you on scheduling.

For some additional background, in September 2022, the County of San Diego Board of Supervisors directed staff to take a proactive, regional approach to address the drought crisis through drought management and water sustainability practices. Our team is leading up the research and recommendations related to various solutions including water recycling, desalination, conservation, storage systems and stormwater capture through the lens of equity. We are currently working with local partners to identify promising ideas and key needs.

Hope to speak with you soon.

Thank you,

Subject: RE: Regional Water Equity Report - Affordable Housing Connection

Dear Monica Hernandez,

I hope you are well.  I’m working as a consultant with LeSar Development Consultants for the County of San Diego to identify ways in which to incentivize affordable housing to utilize sustainable use/reuse of water and stormwater.  This research is part of the County’s anticipated Regional Water Equity Report (the attached fact sheet provides additional context) that will help to inform the County’s larger drought management and water sustainability practices to proactively address the challenges of our region’s reliance on water sources.

We’d like to invite you and others from Casa Familiar to participate in a one-hour (virtual) interview with LDC’s project team and County staff (Elise Ruiz/Group Program Manager with the County’s Land Use and Environment Group).  Our goal is to learn from your experiences in the affordable housing and water conservation/stormwater capture and reuse fields which will help us to identify ways in which to incentivize affordable housing to utilize water conservation/stormwater capture and reuse.  The interview would focus on stormwater infrastructure and affordable housing development process, the financial and regulatory barriers to implementing water and stormwater projects in housing, and potential opportunities to leverage better outcomes in both sectors.  Key themes from the interviews will be summarized in a brief memorandum to County staff.

Please let us know if you (and others from your team) would be willing to join us for a one-hour virtual interview.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

Sincerely,

Danny Serrano, AICP

Hi Elise,

Just checking in on our inquiry below regarding Northern Baja regions to focus on?

Also, please see attached for a revised Stakeholder Interview List that has three phases described below.  I’d like to provide a short summary of our thinking behind this.  The graywater focus interviews are more technical in nature, so we feel like we can get those going sooner than later.  For the Task 2A longer list of stakeholders (15 to be interviewed), we didn’t want to start with too many as there are some decisions that still need to be made regarding the 15 to be interviewed.  Therefore, we only proposed 4 stakeholders on this list where we feel they would provide good input and would take less strategy to establish the interviews.  Most agricultural stakeholders are split between Phase 2 and Phase 3, we think the Phase 2 list could likely be reviewed by your team fairly quickly and would take less messaging strategy (e.g. for the national agriculture stakeholders that were proposed by re-focus).  We anticipate that the local agricultural stakeholders will take more strategy and are therefore listed under Phase 3.

  1.  Phase 1 – these stakeholders would require less strategy on messaging during the interview where Geosyntec/subs could be ready for interview scheduling now.
  2.  Phase 2 – these stakeholders require some strategy, and a meeting between Geosyntec/County is necessary to finalize messaging.
  3.  Phase 3 – these stakeholders require a lot of coordination between Geosyntec/County and require strategic messaging during the interviews.

Let’s plan to discuss this at our standing meeting on Wednesday and any questions you may have.  If possible, I think a good goal would be to get some of these Phase 1 stakeholder interviews going in a week from now to stay on schedule.  I’ll also plan to update the Sharepoint site with this revised matrix.

Thank you,
Stephanie

Subject: RE: Onsite Treatment and Reuse of Non-potable Water

Hi Stephanie,

Below are my notes on the proposed regulations for Onsite Treatment and Reuse of Non-potable Water.

Regulatory Objective

To establish risk-based log reduction targets for the removal of pathogens such as enteric viruses, parasitic protozoa, and enteric bacteria for non-potable water sources (graywater, rainwater, stormwater, and blackwater), and non-potable end uses (toilet and urinal flushing, clothes washing, irrigation, and dust suppression).

Non-potable water sources

Non-potable end uses

*	Graywater
*	Rainwater
*	Stormwater
*	Blackwater

*	Toilet Flushing
*	Clothes Washing
*	Irrigation
*	Dust Suppression

Exclusions

Regulations do not apply to:

*	Untreated graywater systems that are used exclusively for subsurface irrigation
*	Untreated rainwater systems that are used exclusively for surface, subsurface, or drip irrigation
*	Municipal stormwater capture and use systems

What systems are subject to the new regulations?

An onsite treatment system is subject to the new regulations if:

*	It treats one or more of the following water sources, in whole or in part:

	*	Rainwater
	*	Stormwater
	*	Graywater, or
	*	Blackwater

*	The water sources are collected, treated, and used onsite
*	The treated water is used for non-potable purpose
*	It is connected to community sewer system as its only mean for disposal (blackwater system)

The regulations are intended for building-scale or district-scale (multiple buildings or campus) systems onsite reuse.

Risk-based Water Quality Standard

The goal is to achieve a (microbial) risk level of health protection from pathogens in onsite treated water of 1 in 10,000 infections per person per year. This is consistent with acceptable risk for EPA drinking water regulations and State of CA potable reuse regulations.

There will be two sets of log reduction targets for 1) indoor uses (toilet flushing, clothes washing) and 2) outdoor uses (irrigation, dust control, fire suppression, and car washing).

Schedule

The State Water Board is required to adopt the regulations by December 1, 2022. The Department of Housing and Community Development is required to develop and propose for adoption any necessary corresponding building standards to support the regulations adopted by the State Water Board by December 1, 2023.

The State Water Board’s website <https://www.waterboards.ca.gov/drinking_water/certlic/drinkingwater/onsite_nonpotable_reuse_regulations.html>  for the program offers no evidence that the regulation have been finalized. All procedural dates are listed as TBD.

Let me know if you have any questions you’d like me to look into.

Thanks,

Chris

Subject: [External] Onsite Treatment and Reuse of Non-potable Water

Kacen, Stephanie,

Here is some follow-up information from the Policy and Permitting Subcommittee call. The Division of Drinking Water is developing regulations for the Onsite Treatment and Reuse of Non-potable Water. This is a legislative mandate. California Water Code section 13558 requires the State Water Board to adopt regulations on or before December 1, 2022. I just checked the website, and the schedule is still listed as TBD.

There was a workshop earlier this year and several stormwater representatives participated asking a lot of questions about whether this will affect our capture and use projects. The outcome was including the following statement in the FAQ, which is somewhat reassuring, however this might be something to track as the underlying language in the legislation and the draft information shared remains confusing.

12. Will the proposed regulations apply to municipal stormwater capture and use systems? No. The regulations are intended for building-scale or district-scale (multiple buildings or campus) systems onsite reuse. Watershed-scale stormwater capture projects designed to collect and store watershed-wide runoff during dry or wet weather conditions would not fit into the definition of OTNWS since the collection of the source water (stormwater) and in many cases, the use, are not onsite.

See more info here:  https://www.waterboards.ca.gov/drinking_water/certlic/drinkingwater/onsite_nonpotable_reuse_regulations.html <https://www.waterboards.ca.gov/drinking_water/certlic/drinkingwater/onsite_nonpotable_reuse_regulations.html>

subject: Regional Water Equity - April 26th Planning
body:
Hi Lara,

I’m sorry I didn’t have a chance to respond to your Teams message on Thursday – It was a packed day and I’ve been trying to manage the water project with a lot of changes lately.

First, thank you for working on the IRWM contact list, I will be presetting to the RAC this Wednesday, and it will be helpful to continue working with that group as things are moving fast.

The project has been a bit overwhelming, and we are working on a tight timeline to make the April 26th Water Assembly kick-off event come together. One thing that I brought up to Crystal and Stephanie is that we will need a speaker during this program to cover a technical piece concerning the drought status (UCSD was originally scoped for this work but has too much to cover with the literature review). I would like to check in with you to see if you may have any contacts who could fill this role and present a 10-15 minute presentation on April 26th? We would need all material/PPTs ready by April 14th, so I know this is a big ask.

Additionally, if you do not have any contacts, UCSD recommended these potential presenters:

  1.  Jeffrey Mount<https://www.ppic.org/person/jeffrey-mount/>, Public Policy Institute of California (first choice)

He could speak to the drought in terms of long-term trends, provide context for this year, and discuss what is on the horizon, first from a State perspective, but also identifying challenges specific to the RWER region.

  1.  Dr. F. Martin Ralph<https://mralph.scrippsprofiles.ucsd.edu/>, Director, Center for Western Weather Extremes<https://cw3e.ucsd.edu/>, Scripps Institute of Oceanography
Local technical expert on the physical process related to extremes in precipitation, climate projections, etc.

  1.  Luca Delle Monache<https://ldellemonache.scrippsprofiles.ucsd.edu/>, Deputy Director, Center for Western Weather Extremes, Scripps Institute of Oceanography
  2.  Tom Corringham, Research Economist, Center for Western Weather Extremes<https://cw3e.ucsd.edu/>, Scripps Institute of Oceanography

If you have time to secure a person either from this list or from your own recommendation, it would be really helpful to have your support with this task. I have mentioned this to Crystal and Stephanie, so if anyone can secure a presenter let’s keep each other posted.

Please feel free to give me a call this week if that’s easier, and thanks for all your effort on this project!

Elise Ruiz
She/her/ella<https://www.mypronouns.org/>
Group Program Manager
Land Use and Environment Group | County of San Diego
1600 Pacific Highway, Room 212, MS: A-6
San Diego, CA 92101
(619) 455-6865

Subject: Climate Action Research Grant - Letter of Intent (LOI) Due Jan 17th

Hi Everyone:

I hope you are all doing well and had a wonderful holiday season!  I am writing to provide an overview of the Climate Action Research Grant Program and the formation of a San Diego based team, and next steps.

Climate Action Research Grant Program

Just before the holidays in December, the state of California finally released the long awaited call for research (and action) proposals for projects that can demonstrate the ability to hit the ground running and sustain lasting practical and GHG mitigation, reduction and  impacts.  These will be 2 year projects ranging from around 500k up to $10 Million.  A letter of intent (LOI)  is due January 17th which is very soon for projects both with or without matching funds.

We are fortunate to have received a great deal of enthusiasm from all of the partners needed to generate a very competitive application.  The City of San Diego, San Diego County, SANDAG, the Climate Action Campaign, UCSD and other research partners have the ability to form a very strong team with complementary roles and skills that meet the requirements of this RFP.  Each organization has expressed an interest in working together to leverage our collective strengths, expertise, resources, and interests to create a strong and competitive LOI.  It is also possible that we may have the ability to show a significant matching funds by directly supporting other synergistic efforts underway in our region.  Foremost, I will soon be introducing the researchers who will be part of this effort – drawn from several research institutions.

We all share a collective interest and vision for reducing travel and place-based GHG emissions, providing affordable housing, and promoting public health, social justice, and safety through transit and active transportation investments combined with sustainable land use practices.  The policy and regulatory environment is rapidly changing with significant advancements at the state, regional, and local level taking place.  The immediate goal is to craft a compelling LOI that is sufficiently focused and targeted while also being general enough to be something we can all agree to quickly to get the green light from the state to move on to the proposal development stage where we will truly craft our work plan and what we want to accomplish.  There is a tremendous amount of work underway within each of our member organizations to generate a very unique and compelling project.

Next Steps

1.  Confirming who is on our team
2.  Getting your input - convening to discuss focus for LOI – stay tuned
3.  Drafting the AIMS, objectives, approach, and products
4.  Creating budget, timeline, and confirming match
5.  Completing letters of support
6.  Meeting all LOI requirements (see below)
7.  Filing LOI by the 17th
RFP Overview
The RFP can be found at this link: 2023 Request for Proposals (RFP) for the California Climate Action Research Initiative.  “The CA Climate Action Research Grants are intended to spur innovative applied research that addresses California’s climate goals, ensures that local communities are prepared and resilient, and prevents future disasters. This Request for Proposals (RFP) outlines two grant categories: CA Climate Action Seed Grants and CA Climate Action Matching Grants. Proposals for both grant categories must be synergistic with the State of California’s climate action priority or priorities. The California Climate Adaptation Strategy, in particular, presents a holistic vision for the state with the following outcome- based priorities:
1.  Strengthen protections for climate vulnerable communities
2.  Bolster public health and safety to protect against increasing climate risks
3.  Build a climate resilient economy
4.  Accelerate nature-based climate solutions and strengthen climate resilience of natural systems
5.  Make decisions based on the best available climate science
6.  Partner and collaborate to leverage resources
There are several goals and actions under each priority area. Together, this set of priorities requires the participation of multiple disciplines and different types of partners. There are also many other state resources and strategic plans that highlight agency-specific priorities. Appendix A provides a partial list of these resources.  An important emphasis of both grant programs is near-term outcome-based solutions for public impact. (See Sec. 2.4.) To that end, proposal teams must consider thoughtful partnerships, broadly defined based on the proposed project, that will lead to high-impact solutions informed by collective insights and experiences.
Letter of Intent
A letter of intent (LOI) is required for both grant categories. The Applicant PI must specify whether they are applying for a Seed Grant or Matching Grant. Then they must complete the appropriate application materials in the RGPO SmartSimple portal.
Letter of Intent Content. LOI submissions must include the following information:
*   Proposal title (100 characters or less)
*   Identification of Applicant PI and three-page biosketch/CV upload
*   Identification of Co-PIs, Co-Investigators/senior personnel, and other participating personnel
and/or organizations, institutions, or agencies, and a three-page biosketch/CV for each
o IdentifyatleastoneotherCaliforniaacademic/researchinstitutioncollaborator(requiredfor
Matching Grant; encouraged for Seed Grant).
o Identify at least one community/end-user partner (required for Matching Grant; encouraged for
Seed Grant). See Appendix B.
*   Specific California climate priority or priorities the research will address, with links to supporting
agency documents or reports (required). See Appendix A.
*   Actionable outcome(s) expected from the project
*   Abstract/Project Summary addressing the proposed scope of research and activities, rationale, and
potential impact and expected outcomes (2400 characters max)
*   Brief plans for required programmatic components, including collaboration plan, plan for engaging
communities and other end-users, and approach to leveraging available climate related resources,
or infrastructure.
*   Keywords: Research Categories and Identifiers to be selected from a drop-down menu.
*   Seed Grants only: Specific plan for leveraging the Seed Grant during or immediately after grant
period (specific grant or other funding source or opportunity)
*   Matching Grants only: Anticipated contributions for matching commitments (cash and/or in-kind).
See Appendix C.

Greetings All,

I am thrilled to introduce Bethany Facendini, our new Community Engagement and Outreach Manager for the Office of Sustainability and Environmental Justice (OSEJ). Bethany is an experienced community organizer and sustainability advocate, and she will lead our efforts to engage and empower diverse communities throughout our region for climate action.

Bethany will develop and implement strategies to foster community connections and participation in environmental justice and sustainability initiatives. She will work closely with community benefit organizations, leaders, practitioners, and residents to create opportunities for collaboration and partnership.

Bethany brings a wealth of experience and expertise to OSEJ, including numerous community engagement roles in the San Francisco Bay Area and beyond, most recently with Sonoma County Regional Parks as the Community Engagement Division Manager. There, she directed marketing, communications, and cross-sector partnerships, as well as created sustainability and equity-based programs for diverse audiences, community needs assessments, and evaluation systems. In addition, Bethany helped increase the number of culturally relevant programs for under-represented populations (BIPOC, youth impacted by systems, people with disabilities, and families with low incomes). She also served as Sonoma County Human Services’ Community Engagement Manager where she led community programs to increase awareness of services and community outreach events; cultivated relationships between private, governmental, and non-profit organizations to improve partnerships; and built community networks to connect marginalized groups to programs and services. From 2013 – 2015 as the Community Engagement Coordinator for the Sonoma County Department of Health Services, Bethany worked on community engagement and outreach to advance health equity systems change initiatives. She has a Master of Arts in Environmental and Social Justice and a Bachelor of Arts degree in English and LGBTQ Studies. She also has an Urban Environmental Education Certification from Cornell University.

Bethany has world travel and living abroad experience in 46 countries, mostly economically developing nations, and recently returned from a year-long sabbatical traveling solo around the world.

We are excited to have Bethany on board and look forward to her leadership in advancing our environmental justice and sustainability goals. Please join me in welcoming Bethany to our team.

Enjoy the day,

eden

Eden Brukman, Chief Sustainability Officer

Hi Marcus,

I hope you are well.  I’m working as a consultant with LeSar Development Consultants for the County of San Diego to identify ways in which to incentivize affordable housing to utilize sustainable use/reuse of water and stormwater.  This research is part of the County’s anticipated Regional Water Equity Report (the attached fact sheet provides additional context) that will help to inform the County’s larger drought management and water sustainability practices to proactively address the challenges of our region’s reliance on water sources.

We’d like to invite you and others from MAAC (e.g., Christopher Ramirez/Director of Real Estate Development) to participate in a one-hour (virtual) interview with LDC’s project team and County staff (Elise Ruiz/Group Program Manager with the County’s Land Use and Environment Group). The interview would focus on stormwater infrastructure and affordable housing development process, the financial and regulatory barriers to implementing water and stormwater projects in housing, and potential opportunities to leverage better outcomes in both sectors.  Key themes from the interviews will be summarized in a brief memorandum to County staff.

Please let us know if you and Christopher (and others from your team) would be willing to join us for a one-hour virtual interview.

Since Max will already be in attendance he will be available to be the point person on this.

The County is currently evaluating the feasibility of storm drain diversions to water recycling facilities. As such, we are looking to map (via GIS data) local sewer networks and sewersheds draining to water recycling facilities (both direct potable reuse and recycled water [“purple pipe”]). We are also interested in mapping the service areas for all local direct potable reuse facilities, water recycling facilities, and desalination facilities. It would be very helpful if each representative could provide a publicly available data source or identify a subject matter expert (and provide contact information) for more information on obtaining this data.

Thank you for your time and for the thoughtful discussion yesterday! Our team really appreciated the opportunity to connect with you all.

As I mentioned during the meeting, I am happy to meet and discuss the Regional Water Equity effort in more detail. I have attached the Project Fact Sheet and the flyer for the virtual Deep Dive events to share with your communities, and we have these documents translated in the threshold languages, which I can send to you separately.

The Deep Dive series is scheduled through the beginning of September, and we appreciate you sharing the flyer with your networks to inform communities about these events, as their feedback is greatly valued on this topic. You can also refer to the Regional Water Equity website <https://www.sandiegocounty.gov/osej/waterequity/>  to stay informed on upcoming events and project updates. We will continue to stay connected with you and please feel free to let us know if you have any questions.

Have a great evening!

Elise

subject: RE: [External] Re: Climate Action Campaign & Office of Sustainability and EJ Connection
body:
Good morning, Ali,

Thank you very much for creating the time to meet with us! We are looking forward to it.

I sent a scheduler your way for Monday from 1-2pm at Better Buzz in Hillcrest. We mainly want to get to know you and how we can work more effectively together on this project as we go forward. We can also touch on the next steps for our collective effort for the RDF’s Water Equity project, including the Water Assembly.

Here are some of the action items we captured from our meeting (please feel free to add to these):

*	COSD staff will review the outreach reports you previously sent to colleagues by 7/24 (BF, ER, JB)
*	COSD staff will glean water related data provided by stakeholders from the reports by 8/1 (ER, JB)
*	Bethany will set-up next in person meeting with Ali by 7/18
*	Elise will send Ali the survey questions to integrate into the existing RDF survey by 7/18; Ali will distribute the three-question survey out to stakeholder distribution list by ?
*	COSD will identify a presenter for the San Diego Green New Deal Alliance meeting on August 28, 5:30-7:30pm, and coordinate the details with Ali by 8/1
*	Ali will sent a list of the anticipated outreach presentation details for the next month to Bethany by ?
*	COSD staff will create an enewsletter submission to Ali for CAC distribution by ?

Please let me know if you have any questions or suggestions.

Have a beautiful day, Ali!

Bethany

Bethany Facendini, Community Engagement and Outreach Manager

Pronouns: she/her/hers

>
>
> Dear Members of the Board,
>
> As mentioned at the Board of Directors meeting last Friday, I wanted to
> provide an update on two pieces of legislation recently introduced in the
> state legislature that, if enacted, would modify the composition of the
> SANDAG Board of Directors:
>
> *AB 24 (DeMaio)*
> This bill, introduced by Assemblymember Carl DeMaio, proposes modifying
> the SANDAG Board of Directors by removing one of the two County Board of
> Supervisors seats and replacing it with a representative from the San Diego
> County Association of Planning Groups. It would also require the remaining
> County Board representative to be from an unincorporated area of the
> county. The bill has been double-referred to the Assembly Local Government
> Committee and the Assembly Transportation Committee. It currently does not
> have a scheduled hearing date.
>
> *SB 240 (Jones)*
> This bill, introduced by Senate Minority Leader Brian Jones, proposes to
> replace the secondary representative from the County Board of Supervisors
> with a resident from an unincorporated area of the County, as selected by a
> majority of the county’s community planning groups, to serve a 1-year term.
> The bill also eliminates the requirement that one Board of Supervisors
> member be from a substantially incorporated district and the other from an
> unincorporated district. This bill has not yet been referred to a policy
> committee in the Senate.
>
> We will continue to monitor these bills and provide you with updates
> accordingly.
>
> Thank you,
> Mario
>

subject: CPSG invite to upcoming meetings for Cannabis Program Draft EIR
body:
Hello CPSG Chairs,

Yesterday you should have received a GovDelivery notice announcing that the Draft Program Environmental Impact Report (Draft EIR) and draft ordinances for the proposed Socially Equitable Cannabis Program (Cannabis Program) are now available for public review through March 31, 2025.

We have made the documents available for review and comment on the Engage San Diego County Cannabis Program Environmental Impact Report page<https://engage.sandiegocounty.gov/cannabis-program-eir>. This feature allows people to view and provide their comments directly into the draft documents.

We have also created several fact sheets about the Draft EIR and ordinances to assist in your review - you can find these under "Documents" on the Engage page linked above and attached:

  *   Draft EIR Fact Sheet
  *   Draft EIR - How to Comment Tip Sheet
  *   Draft Zoning Ordinance Fact Sheet
  *   Draft Regulatory Code Fact Sheet

I wanted to personally invite you and the other members of your groups to attend one of our upcoming public comment meetings and open houses.

Virtual Meetings

  *   When:
*       February 5, 2025, 6:00 p.m.
*       February 6, 2025, 6:00 p.m.
*       February 12, 2025, 6:00 p.m.

  *   Zoom Link: https://us06web.zoom.us/j/84368497586?pwd=RVAZurGJyguieIv4Mo2IkuqgRq1zob.1<https://links-2.govdelivery.com/CL0/https:%2F%2Fus06web.zoom.us%2Fj%2F84368497586%3Fpwd=RVAZurGJyguieIv4Mo2IkuqgRq1zob.1/1/01010194b9a95fa0-bd5a76eb-9462-4664-aff2-a37cb9a5a674-000000/I7mLl-wiCplNGHINWsFRSjoE918tTdgMyKlfA5t18LA=390>

In-Person Open Houses

  *   When & Where:
*       February 25, 2025, 5:30 - 7:30 p.m., Lakeside County Library, 12428 Woodside Avenue, Lakeside, CA 92040
*       February 26, 2025, 5:30 - 7:30 p.m., Valley Center County Library, 29200 Cole Grade Road, Valley Center, CA 92082

At the virtual comment meetings, we will discuss what is included in Draft EIR and ordinances and the public review process and provide an opportunity for the public to provide verbal comments on the draft documents. The in-person open house events will provide an opportunity to talk to representatives from the County and submit your comments.  Please note, all comments received at these meetings will become part of the official public record.

Please don't hesitate to reach out to me directly with any questions - my contact information is in my signature box below.

Thank you,

With our CPSGs reviewing the County's Cannabis Program EIR and compiling their concerns over the program alternatives, the Jamul Dulzura CPG felt it important to share this particular concern that Kathleen Lippitt recently provided us with the entire APG.  Please see below....

The smell of weed is wreaking havoc across California
The state's largest indoor cannabis farm is under fire thanks to the "disgusting" smell of pot
By Lester Black, Cannabis editorMarch 5, 2025

David Bernard, left, the COO of C4 USA, said the company plans to push forward with an expansion even as neighbors complain about cannabis odor.
Courtesy of C4 USA
California is globally synonymous with cannabis, but the plant’s distinctive smell has become a major headache for people across the state.
From Northern California to the desert to the coast, California residents have been complaining for years that the smell of legal cannabis farms is destroying their quality of life. And in some places, local governments are beginning to act.

In Cathedral City, a small enclave near Palm Springs, the city council approved a moratorium last week that will block any new cannabis businesses from opening or expanding after years of complaints over cannabis odors. The moratorium was aimed directly at Cat City Cannabis Co., a massive indoor marijuana cultivation facility that has generated complaints for years from nearby residents who say the facility emits a “disgusting” smell.
Mayor Pro Tem Raymond Gregory said during the meeting that the moratorium would stop the facility from expanding further.

“That won’t affect what we’re going to be continuing to work with on the current issue, but it will stop them building a whole ’nother building,” Gregory said.

David Bernard, the COO of C4 USA, which owns the facility, said in an emailed statement to SFGATE that they are actively working with the city to develop an “effective odor management solution” but that they are also pushing forward with their phase 2 expansion. It will add 168,000 square feet of space to the existing 325,000-square-foot facility, which is already the largest indoor pot farm in the state, according to the company’s website.
“Though the moratorium has impacted our timeline, we view this as an opportunity to work collaboratively with the city and the local community to develop a long-term, effective odor management solution,” Bernard said.

The Cathedral City action comes after the Santa Barbara County Planning Commission unanimously recommended last month that all greenhouse cannabis growers install carbon filters within a year. The area near the coastal town of Carpinteria is a major hub for greenhouse cannabis growers, and residents have been complaining about the “sewer-like” smell of cannabis for years. The recommendation still needs to be approved by the county’s Board of Supervisors before it becomes law.

Some of the greenhouses have already installed the filtration systems, which can cost millions of dollars, while others have installed misting systems that attempt to camouflage the smell of fresh marijuana, although those systems have been panned as making entire neighborhoods smell like laundromats.
Most agricultural companies are protected from neighborhood complaints over nuisances like odor through so-called “Right to Farm” laws, but most local governments, including Santa Barbara’s, have exempted cannabis farms from receiving those protections.

Some California residents are saying the smell of cannabis is more than just a nuisance and that it could actually be causing health problems. The Sonoma Neighborhood Coalition, a group that is critical of cannabis policies, has been pushing for the county to ban outdoor cannabis farms entirely because, according to the group, pot plants release toxic chemicals including beta-myrcene. In December, the group warned against allowing outdoor cannabis farms, saying allowing pot farms would be “assaulting your right to defend your home from businesses that spew carcinogens into your yard and your house.”

Beta-myrcene is a naturally occurring compound found in thousands of plants. Studies have shown it can have carcinogenic effects when exposed at high levels, but SFGATE was not able to independently verify if cannabis farms would ever produce enough of the chemical to meet those toxic levels to nearby residents. Hops also produce the compound, and there do not appear to be problems in Yakima Valley where over 50,000 acres of hops are planted every year.

In Cathedral City, the smell of cannabis has tainted what was originally a genial relationship between the town and the pot industry. Locals were ecstatic when plans for the Cat City Cannabis Co. facility were first announced in 2018, with the planning commission unanimously approving the project and local neighbors telling the Desert Sun that they were happy a long vacant lot was becoming a job creator. The facility, which ballooned in price to $120 million, traded hands before opening under its current ownership.

Now, the mood is decidedly angry. Debbie Price, a local resident, told the council that “we are all flipping trapped” and called for an injunction to cease operations immediately until “there is no smell.”

“Is Cathedral City slated to be another Salton Sea area? You may laugh, but you know what, so did they,” Price said.
Gregory, the mayor pro tem, said that the council would have acted differently in 2020 if they knew about the smell and directed the company to end the odor.

“Stop the odor, and we’ll be done,” Gregory said.

Lester Black
CANNABIS EDITOR
Lester Black is SFGATE's cannabis editor. He was born in Torrance, raised in Seattle, and has written for FiveThirtyEight.com, High Country News, The Guardian, The Albuquerque Journal, The Tennessean, and many other publications. He was previously the cannabis columnist for The Stranger.

--

Kathleen M. Lippitt, MPH

Public Health Practitioner
