subject: Report on SANDAG's January 2025 Meetings to the Association of Planning Groups - San Diego County
body:
Good Afternoon APG Members,

Note: The SANDAG Board of Directors held three meetings in the month of
January.

*SANDAG Leadership Changes - New Officers Elected:*
New Chair for SANDAG BOD: Lesa Heebner, City of Solana Beach
New Vice Chair for SANDAG BOD: Joe Lacava, City of San Diego
New Second Vice Chair for SANDAG BOD: John Minto, City of Santee

Jan. 10th - APG comment to Board: Good morning. Congratulations on your
election as the dream team for the officers. I do represent the
unincorporated area, over 500,000 people, and, of course, this seat is not
a voting seat. Today I want to note for the record that the County is not
present and so, therefore; all action taken by this Board today - voting
action - has effectively disenfranchised the Unincorporated Area. We're not
present. And, we don't have a vote. And, I hope in 2025, I expect in 2025,
that this Board will overall do a better job of ensuring that the
Unincorporated Area is not disenfranchised. I realize County being absent
is not the fault of the Board, but there must be something in place that
takes into account that there's over half a million people who are not
participating in the proceedings today. Thank you.

Jan. 31st - APG Comment to the Board: The County of San Diego is not
present. However, the people of the County of San Diego are present.
(Note: County was completely absent for all of the January 2025 BOD
meetings - 10th & 24th & 31st)

*SANDAG CEO, Mario Orso Report:*
-Mario Orso reported that the CFO was adjusting revenue projections on
TransNet funds by a couple of percentage points - between 2 to 4%. This
would be a decrease in expected funding and could affect both MTS and NCTD.
-The Grand Jury report findings and recommendations came as no surprise as
the Office of the Independent Performance Auditor had brought these needed
issues and changes to the Board in their earlier report and they are being
addressed.

*Otay Mesa East and SR 11 Report:*
The Federal agreements with U.S. Customs and Border Protection and with
General Services have set the stage for the beginning of construction and
the relationship SANDAG will have with CBP. Caltrans is also a partner.
If the toll revenues of the Port of Entry are not as projected the
shortfall cannot be made up with TransNet funds.

Ann Fox, Caltrans comment: ...We've done the studies that have shown the
many dollars and jobs lost and the air pollution created by the long delays
along our shared borders. California has invested more than half of the
$1.3 billion project cost and has spent hundreds of millions more building
out the corridor and the connections we have with State Routes 905 and 125.
...We have built the infrastructure, the new roads, the utilities, the
technology, the air quality monitors out there, in addition to over 180
acres of environmental mitigation.

Jack Fisher, City of Imperial Beach comment: (reading Brian Bilbray letter)
"... I'm sure some other members will not continue to support the expansion
of the economic growth with the environmental damage without addressing
historical and future environmental and public health threats caused by
such economic development. I ask that every board member here question if
their city council or county board would vote for any project knowing its
environmental and health problems if it was going to be anywhere close to
the disastrous situation that citizens of the South Bay faced everyday?"
I can't tell you how frustrated I am because I know with the increased
traffic and commerce Mexico will continue to grow. Their population will
continue to grow. It was mentioned that just this operation port of entry
opening will create 90,000 jobs on the U.S. side. I would imagine that
number probably doubles or triples on the Mexico side. Still without the
infrastructure.

*TransNet Major Corridor Projects Update: State Route 67:*
Sam Amen, Karina Cantera-Angel & Tracy D'Aoust Roberts of Caltrans -
presented 3 alternatives for the improvement of SR 67 understanding that
evacuation was the highest consideration. Project area is SR 67 from
Highland Valley in Ramona to Mapleview in Lakeside. Alternative #1 provides
4 outbound lanes and one inbound lane dedicated to inbound emergency
vehicles. Alternatives #2 & #3 provide some of these benefits, but not
consistently throughout the project area and include the use of shoulders
as "lanes" in an emergency.

APG comment to Board: The Unincorporated Area has been partnering with
Caltrans and we thank Sam, Karina, Tracy, Melina, Stephen and Tyler for
their dedication. Safety is always first.  Caltrans states, "The primary
goal of the SR 67 Highway Improvements Project is to increase capacity
during emergencies to significantly reduce evacuation times."  Safety is
always first. SANDAG serves over 3.3 million people across the region;
however, some benefit more than others. Had SANDAG delivered on the
promises of TransNet to the Unincorporated Area - Measure G would have
passed. The experience of those patiently awaiting their turn at the
Regional funding bucket has been disheartening. 1988 and 2004 turned into a
resounding "no" in 2024 for rural communities on Measure G. The LA fires
demonstrate a clear and present danger to rural highway travelers -
evacuees may live locally or may be visiting from the city. Caltrans has
stood ready and willing to deliver highway safety. Alternative #1 delivers
on the Promise. Let us immediately put into place emergency widening to
move evacuees through the current SR 67 gauntlet of bottlenecks. Safety is
always first. SANDAG does not want to be the obstacle to improvements
necessary to avoid the catastrophic results of the LA fires. The elected
Board members would not want the public to rightfully be able to say that
they could have done more to prevent a loss of life and property. Thank you.

Steve Vaus, City of Poway; Carolina Chavez, City of Chula Vista; Rebecca
Jones, City of San Marcos; Kevin Shin, City of Carlsbad; Bill Wells, City
of El Cajon; John Minto, City of Santee;  & Terry Gaasterland, City of Del
Mar all made comments: All of these city representatives were positive in
their comments emphasizing the need to expand SR 67 for evacuation purposes
and Mayors Minto, Jones, Wells and Gaasterland specifically endorsed the
selection of Alternative #1. There were no comments opposing Caltrans
proposed solutions to SR 67. The Board of Directors was supportive.

Lesa Heebner, City of Solana Beach & SANDAG Chair comment:  "What can we do
now?"

Allan Kosup, Caltrans response: We have an emergency widening project that
just began this week on SR 67. The environmental report was received last
week and the project was begun immediately. It will be over the next six
months. This will provide more space in the event of an evacuation.

*APG News:*
-Thank you to all who were able to attend our in-person APG meeting held on
Saturday, January 4th, 2025. A quorum was established and voting actions
were taken.

*APG Officers elected for 2025 (one year terms):*
Chair, Robin Joy Maxson
Vice Chair, Eileen Delaney
Secretary, Carol Hake

*APG Representative to SANDAG Board of Directors (two year terms):*
Primary Representative, Robin Joy Maxson
Alternate Representative, Eileen Delaney

*APG Representatives to SANDAG Policy Advisory Committees:*

Regional Planning Committee:
APG Representative: Ron Nehring
APG Alternate: Kiki Skagen Munshi

Transportation Committee:
APG Representative: Jim Custeau
APG Alternate: Paul Dombkowski

Borders Committee:
APG Representative: Lynne Malinowski
APG Alternate: Harriet Taylor

Public Safety Committee:
APG Representative: Paul Dombkowski
APG Alternate: Eileen Delaney

Audit Committee:
APG Representative: Carol Hake

-Update: Congressman Darrell Issa - representing the majority of the
unincorporated area in San Diego County - has not set a meeting date with
the APG as of this report. Since July, the APG has been working to set up a
joint meeting with the Congressman, SANDAG CEO Mario Orso and our APG
members without success. SANDAG CEO Mario Orso has stated he will be
available and happy to attend our joint meeting. Congressman Issa has not
been available and very little communication has come from his office. The
APG sent a request to his Chief of Staff, Veronica Smith Wong. She has
responded, but not with a set date, yet.

The subject of the meeting will be:
"Transportation funding and safety in the Unincorporated Area; addressing
fatality rate on rural highways, safe wildfire evacuation, lack of public
transportation resulting in geographic isolation of vulnerable populations
and continued diversion of transportation funds from rural highway
projects."

Several Planning/Sponsor Groups have already sent letters to Congressman
Issa. If any group wishes to contact Issa directly, email his Chief of
Staff Veronica Smith Wong: veronica.smith@mail.house.gov

*Questions from APG members*
No questions received this month.

*Links*
SANDAG BOD and PAC meetings for calendar 2025:
https://legistarweb-production.s3.amazonaws.com/uploads/attachment/pdf/3108009/Item_3_-_Revised_2025_Legislative_Calendar.pdf

Original SANDAG documents and meeting minutes are available directly from
SANDAG's Board of Directors website:
https://www.sandag.org/meetings-and-events/board-of-directors

Report Submitted by:
Robin Joy Maxson, Representative to SANDAG
Association of Planning Groups - San Diego County

subject: Re: Loveland Trail Improvements Meeting 3/14
body:
Nicholas Brust

Deputy District Director

CA Senator Brian Jones

Good Morning, Mr. Brust,

Thank you for working on this meeting for the trails and other Loveland community priorities, such as fish restocking, reasonable public access hours that server working people and families, and a balance of recreation and wildlife protection in conjunction with water storage policies.

I would like to add that some things are not allowed : 

1}Contractors interested in bidding projects are excluded from steering the proposals.

2)Proposals that push AB 1O2 funds through any brand, for instance, a nonprofit or commercial interest.

One exception might be costs associated with paperwork or title work/  an escrow to incorporate the SDGE easements into public access trails. 

What I would like to suggest:

1) Before the meeting: Clarity from Congressman Issa's office on the legality and restoration of  Forest Service easement-protected hours of Sunrise to Sunset and the encumbrance of the fishing program on Sweetwater's minimum pool. 

2) Invite an SDGE public affairs specialist to discuss the public use of the  Sunrise Powerlink easement roads at Loveland.

3) A neutral subject matter expert contractor on trails, fishing infrastructure,  and other related matters who is in an advisory role only and will not unduly steer or bid on proposals.

4) Participation from a  Regional Waterboards  permitting expert to help define or give feedback on impacts that water regulation standards will or won’t have on our proposals. Confusion on these matters has been stifling in previous meetings.

5) A rubric for choosing proposals created by the Loveland stakeholders in attendance or designed by Mr. Jantz with consideration for feedback from Sweetwater Authority and Loveland advocates/stakeholders.

Please let me know if I can assist you or others in Senator Jones's office with this important meeting. 

Appreciatively,

Russell Walsh

4639 Montiel Truck Trail

Jamul CA, 91935

619-922-6235

subject: UPDATE ON COUNTY OF SAN DIEGO VEHICLE MILES TRAVELED MITIGATION PROGRAM
body:
Dear Interested Stakeholder,

We want to update you on our progress to implement the Board of Supervisors (Board) direction related to a Vehicle Miles Traveled (VMT) mitigation program.

On March 1, 2023, the Board received a report on VMT mitigation program options and provided direction to continue coordination with outside agencies and jurisdictions, to estimate costs to project applicants, to solicit stakeholder input, and to receive additional Board direction before the VMT mitigation program is fully developed.

A VMT mitigation program will play a role in determining where development efforts are focused in the unincorporated area, such as near jobs and transit to reduce travel and greenhouse gas emissions, consistent with the intent of Senate Bill (SB) 743, balanced with considerations regarding development feasibility.

On May 22, 2024, staff will provide an update to the Board on the development of the VMT mitigation program and options that staff are evaluating as part of the program.

Two public meetings options are available to learn about the development of a VMT mitigation program.

Public Meeting 1 (Virtual)

When: April 18, 2024 at 5:30pm

Link to Join: https://us06web.zoom.us/j/85959265420
                       Meeting ID: 859 5926 5420

Public Meeting 2 (In-Person)

When: April 23, 2024 at 6:30 pm

Where: County Operations Center Chambers
               5520 Overland Avenue

               San Diego, CA 92123

Disability-related accommodations necessary to facilitate meeting participation, language interpretation, including American Sign Language, and/or written materials in alternative languages and formats are available upon request. Please submit your request at least 72 hours in advance of the event to Damon Davis at damon.davis@sdcounty.ca.gov<mailto:damon.davis@sdcounty.ca.gov>.

We are also reaching out specifically to your individual groups as you have previously requested meetings or expressed interest in the County's ongoing implementation of VMT policies, as well as identifying your group as an area of interest related to our current efforts associated with potential VMT mitigation programs.  In addition to the announced Public Meetings, if you group would like to request an individual meeting with County staff, please contact Damon Davis at damon.davis@sdcounty.ca.gov<mailto:damon.davis@sdcounty.ca.gov>, and we will coordinate an in-person or virtual meeting at your convenience.

Thank you,

body:
Good afternoon and happy Friday – It is great to e-meet you, Melissa and Corey!

We really appreciate your interest in this effort, as we value insight from USGBC to help inform our research on the important topic of water sustainability.

We are currently in the phase of developing the comprehensive report with the support of our consulting team, and hosting outreach events to gather feedback from our communities. I want to share a few resources with you to give you some details about the Regional Water Equity effort.

*	I’ve attached a project fact sheet which gives background details on this effort, which was directed by our Board of Supervisors, and how we are researching focus area by topic.
*	Please check out the Regional Water Equity website <https://www.sandiegocounty.gov/content/sdc/lueg/osej/regional_water_equity_project.html>  as well to learn about what has been done so far and what steps we have planned next.

Would your team be available to meet for a 1-hour interview sometime in the next month? We can provide interview questions ahead of time so you can prepare. If you could provide some timeframes, I would happy to coordinate a meeting that would work best for your team’s availability. Again, thank you for your time to collaborate with us and we look forward to connecting!

All the best,

Elise Ruiz, Group Program Manager

*	Integrated approaches to develop climate resilient solutions which support vulnerable populations and maintain biodiversity

Hi Elise,

Just checking in on our inquiry below regarding Northern Baja regions to focus on?

Also, please see attached for a revised Stakeholder Interview List that has three phases described below.  I’d like to provide a short summary of our thinking behind this.  The graywater focus interviews are more technical in nature, so we feel like we can get those going sooner than later.  For the Task 2A longer list of stakeholders (15 to be interviewed), we didn’t want to start with too many as there are some decisions that still need to be made regarding the 15 to be interviewed.  Therefore, we only proposed 4 stakeholders on this list where we feel they would provide good input and would take less strategy to establish the interviews.  Most agricultural stakeholders are split between Phase 2 and Phase 3, we think the Phase 2 list could likely be reviewed by your team fairly quickly and would take less messaging strategy (e.g. for the national agriculture stakeholders that were proposed by re-focus).  We anticipate that the local agricultural stakeholders will take more strategy and are therefore listed under Phase 3.

  1.  Phase 1 – these stakeholders would require less strategy on messaging during the interview where Geosyntec/subs could be ready for interview scheduling now.
  2.  Phase 2 – these stakeholders require some strategy, and a meeting between Geosyntec/County is necessary to finalize messaging.
  3.  Phase 3 – these stakeholders require a lot of coordination between Geosyntec/County and require strategic messaging during the interviews.

Let’s plan to discuss this at our standing meeting on Wednesday and any questions you may have.  If possible, I think a good goal would be to get some of these Phase 1 stakeholder interviews going in a week from now to stay on schedule.  I’ll also plan to update the Sharepoint site with this revised matrix.

Thank you,

Stephanie

Subject: San Diego County Regional Water Equity Report (RWER)

Good afternoon Mr. Roy,

Thank you for your time this morning. I am following up with information about the Regional Water Equity Assessment/Report. As I mentioned to you over the phone, we are at the tail end of stakeholder interviews and would love to get your interview included in our report by the 31st of May. I have attached a fact sheet on the project and the interview questions that we would like to ask you with our GeoSyntec consultants if you are able to participate. I have cc’d Elise Ruiz who is the lead of this project in the Office of Sustainability and Environmental Justice.

Essentially, this process of assessing what communities are/are not able to do to reach water equity in terms of sustainability through stormwater capturing, wastewater systems, and greywater strategies will provide a report to the County Board of Supervisors this September. We see this report being a reference to future policy and potential funding.

I saw that you accepted the calendar invite for Thursday the 25th at 2:00 p.m. to meet with Elise and me. If you find that you might be available to do the interview then, we could a lot more time and check with GeoSyntecs availability.

Thank you again!

From: Daniel Serrano <Daniel@lesardevelopment.com>
Sent: Thursday, May 25, 2023 2:52 PM
To: Choi, Michael <michael.choi@kimley-horn.com>
Cc: Ruiz, Elise <Elise.Ruiz@sdcounty.ca.gov>
Subject: RE: Regional Water Equity Report - Affordable Housing Connection

Dear Michael Choi,

I hope you are well.  I’m working as a consultant with LeSar Development Consultants for the County of San Diego to identify ways in which to incentivize affordable housing to utilize sustainable use/reuse of water and stormwater.  This research is part of the County’s anticipated Regional Water Equity Report (the attached fact sheet provides additional context) that will help to inform the County’s larger drought management and water sustainability practices to proactively address the challenges of our region’s reliance on water sources.

We’d like to invite you as well as local KHA staff in the San Diego area to participate in a one-hour (virtual) interview with LDC’s project team and County staff (Elise Ruiz/Group Program Manager with the County’s Land Use and Environment Group).  Our goal is to learn from your experiences in the affordable housing and water conservation/stormwater capture and reuse fields which will help us to identify ways in which to incentivize affordable housing to utilize water conservation/stormwater capture and reuse.  The interview would focus on stormwater infrastructure and affordable housing development process, the financial and regulatory barriers to implementing water and stormwater projects in housing, and potential opportunities to leverage better outcomes in both sectors.  Key themes from the interviews will be summarized in a brief memorandum to County staff.

Please let us know if you (and others from your team) would be willing to join us for a one-hour virtual interview.

Thank you for your time and consideration.

Sincerely,

Danny Serrano, AICP

Greetings Ken,

Thank you for making time to connect with me earlier today. This email is intended to summarize our conversation; please let me know if you have any corrections.

As you know, Geosyntec has subcontracted an aspect of work for the County of San Diego’s Regional Water Equity Report to UCSD. It was brought to my attention that a staff member from UCSD has been acting in an unprofessional manner, using hostile and discriminatory language toward a County employee and making them feel uncomfortable and unsafe due to the outbursts. This behavior is not tolerated by the County, and we appreciate your timely attention to remove any direct contact between UCSD staff and County employees moving forward. As UCSD is not a primary member of the project team, it is not anticipated that this change will compromise the quality of product that Geosyntec is providing to the Report.

During the County’s investigation of the situation, one of Geosyntec’s staff shared that she, too, felt targeted by the UCSD staff’s behavior and comments. As she is a Geosyntec employee, we expect that your office will perform whatever investigation you deem necessary.

We do hope that Geosyntec will communicate with UCSD the reasons for the change, so that the individual might be held accountable by their employer and get the help that they need.

I appreciate your help in addressing this matter.

Sincerely~
eden

Legally-established water rights have long been a foundation for allocation and adjudication of access to water in California. subject: RE: Deep Dive Thoughts
body:
Oops, was just informed that we did use a zoom slide (thanks, Jacob) – I totally missed it. My apologies!

From: Appel, Rebeca
Sent: Thursday, July 13, 2023 10:49 AM
To: Ruiz, Elise <Elise.Ruiz@sdcounty.ca.gov>
Cc: Boerboom, Jacob <Jacob.Boerboom@sdcounty.ca.gov>
Subject: Deep Dive Thoughts

Good morning Elise,

Great job yesterday! There was a lot of on-the-fly decisions and pivoting on the event, so huge kudos to you for navigating it all so smoothly. I think the team also did a great job and there were some really insightful comments made by our participants (going back our conversation about pulling quotes for the report – these deep dives could be a great way to grab some quotes from!) ??

I did have a few thoughts that I wanted to share for your consideration (my apologies, I had some of these thoughts after the first deep dive, but had to leave our debrief early):

*	Consider allowing ~3-4 minutes to let folks join the meeting so they do not miss the intro also ensure to read the cover slide and welcome folks to “Deep Dive: XXX (bring in the title)” – help set the stage to the specific topic
*	Consider using these zoom slides ( TEMPLATE RDF_Implementation Playbook Slides for Working Groups.pptx <https://sdcountycagov.sharepoint.com/:p:/s/LUEG-OSEJ/ESa-zjxsJxFEtT1NUIYgRasB03yTCE3-N87n_OW6KvFOIg?e=Ex8hTm> ) for introducing using zoom, chat, and there is in interpreter - folks need to click the globe (at the bottom of the zoom platform)

	*	I know most are familiar with zoom but its helpful and this would also help allow some time for folks to join and not miss the great content of the RWER and the presenter

*	I also think it would be good to say that “this meeting is being recorded and will be posted on our website for future viewing” (or something along those lines). I know zoom notifies participants, but it is still good to say it and verbally let folks know why.

Please let me know if you have any questions at all or would like to discuss. It has been great to be on these as a team and engage directly with folks. Hope you have a great Friday-eve!

Rebeca Appel, Group Program Manager

(she, her, ella)

Office of Sustainability and Environmental Justice

County of San Diego Land Use and Environment Group

Hi Chris,

I need some help developing a set of FAQs for the upcoming Water Assembly (outreach) for the Water Equity Report. It's ok to develop more questions that fewer, and copy existing FAQs we have developed, as we plan to refine the list during an upcoming meeting.

The attached "fact sheet" is draft (so isn't for distribution yet) but includes a few dot-points that can provide you some context for the type of information we'll share during the Water Assembly. The FAQs we discussed developing would be considered "low handing fruit" (not complex questions or in the weeds) and focus on questions we anticipate stakeholders may ask on local water needs, water equity, reliability, and supply including stormwater harvesting or capture/reuse.

We have FAQs on our website, and the IRWM program website www.sdirwmp.org <http://www.sdirwmp.org> ; these would be a good starting point. Of course, if you need further guidance, please reach out to me; we need a draft by Tuesday of next week (mid-day would be great).

Best,

Subject: RE: Response to Concerns (County RDF): NAACP North San Diego County

Dear Satia and Sonia,
On behalf of the Office of Sustainability and Environmental Justice (Office), we would like to congratulate Satia on your recent award for community service in the city of Oceanside, in the honor Dr. Martin Luther King, Jr. We applaud your long-time efforts to engage the youth and in the furtherance of racial justice.
We have received your letter on behalf of NAACP North San Diego County (NSDC).  Thank you for applauding the County’s efforts with the Regional Decarbonization Framework. I appreciate the attention NAACP NSDC is bringing to important equity considerations and look forward to being able to address your concerns.
By way of background, our Office was created by Board direction to have a regional lens on both sustainability as well as environmental justice. The founding principle of our Office is to address past and present injustices, and to ensure that these injustices do not occur in the future. We are in the process of establishing the programs of this Office and would truly appreciate working with you on this. You can find more information about us at: Office of Sustainability and Environmental Justice (sandiegocounty.gov)<https://www.sandiegocounty.gov/content/sdc/lueg/Office-of-Environmental-and-Climate-Justice/>
Our flagship project - the Regional Decarbonization Framework (RDF) - supports our visionary goal of reaching zero carbon emissions by 2045 or sooner in the San Diego region, and it is based on the guiding principles of science-based pathways, regional collaboration and community engagement centered on equity. The work on this framework began with Board direction in January 2021, and with Board direction in April, will continue until we no longer have a climate crisis in the region. We sincerely appreciate the participation of NAACP NSDC leadership in this project, some of whom I have known and admired for their heroic advocacy for many years.
The County’s strategic initiatives span across the entire organization, break down silos and set measurable goals on sustainability, community, equity, empowerment, and justice. Our Board of Supervisors has broken down historical barriers to inclusivity and participation through strong leadership in policies and programs.  This is my own calling to be part of this transformation. I strongly believe that equity is the key to sustainability<http://web.mit.edu/dusp/dusp_extension_unsec/projections/issue_8/issue_8_baxamusa.pdf>, and that we cannot address climate change without meaningful participation of all communities. Our RDF team’s innovative work on community outreach through new forums, venues and tools of community engagement, new forms of partnerships with community-based organizations, and the new ways of access to experts and technical material, demonstrate our commitment to the founding principles of our Office.
However, we recognize that more can and should be done and are grateful for the points raised in your letter to the County Board of Supervisors. Here are some of our initial thoughts on the questions that you raise:
Engagement for the Technical Study:
The technical study authored by a team of experts led by UC San Diego School of Global Policy & Strategy began their work in July 2021 and have updated the Board of Supervisors and the public five times over this period. Three drafts of the Regional Decarbonization Framework Technical Report were prepared followed by public comment and review periods, focus groups, as well as concurrent reviews by a Technical Work Group on each draft. We had workshops on every topic last year, and the authors discussed their findings with a variety of stakeholders. A summary of this report has been available online on the RDF website<https://www.sandiegocounty.gov/content/sdc/sustainability/regional-decarbonization/projects.html>, in eight languages since the very beginning. The RDF team appreciates the participation of NAACP NSDC leaders in the development of the technical study.
Engagement for the Implementation Playbook:
The Playbook is the first-ever user-friendly compilation of best practices that resulted from an inventory of climate action measures/activities in all Climate Action Plan (CAP) in the region. It is being supplemented by stakeholder and community feedback on activities that need to be included, as well as case studies locally or from other regions. By making this resource available to the public, we hope that it will guide future CAP updates for all jurisdictions in the San Diego region and serve as a living resource informed by the learned experiences of individuals, communities, businesses, and agencies. Work to shape the Playbook began in August last year starting with a co-design process by working groups tailored to the five sectors that were studied. We organized regional convenings by each Supervisorial District to provide a basic understanding of the impacts of climate change on public health in the region and how we can get communities to be engaged in the implementation activities for climate mitigation and resiliency.
Public comment has always been welcome on the RDF throughout our process. We receive comments through our website, Engage platform<https://engage.sandiegocounty.gov/rdf>, emails, phone calls and meetings, and will continue to receive input and comments throughout the development and implementation of the RDF. The meeting presentation for the regional convenings were posted in advance on our website on January 15, translated in all 8 threshold languages. District 3 residents could view the publicly posted materials in an accessible format, as well as participate in any of the regional convenings, both in person or virtually. The intent of having a convening physically located within a Supervisorial District was to increase access to residents throughout our vast region that want to attend a meeting in person. We also received written comments from Sonja on February 1, to whom we are appreciative for participating in person at the District 5 regional convening. We understand the hardship of the cancelled event in District 3 beyond our control and worked to reschedule it at the earliest date that the speakers were available.
The County released a partial draft on the Framework’s Implementation Playbook in January, and our team is currently incorporating some recommended information and public comments on the initial draft. The public comment period for that partial initial draft has been extended to March 31 to reflect community input that will serve as a basis for a newly scheduled Board meeting discussion on April 5. Public comment will continue throughout the implementation process and to help the region reach its goals our efforts will continue evolve and reflect best practices available in current regulatory and technical environments. Following the April Board discussion on the Playbook, we will take it back out into area neighborhoods to explore possibilities, get reactions and suggestions from the community.  This fall, we are planning a second series of regional convenings by supervisorial district as well as in tribal lands. This series of convenings will be focused on community-driven implementation activities. To bolster participation, please send us recommendations of people you would like included.
It is important to note that the County is not recommending or mandating any particular activity in the Playbook. This is a collective knowledge base that needs to be continually informed by some of the climate-related activities that are already occurring in frontline communities. The work to date is just the beginning of our journey to decarbonize the region, and the success of this effort depends on active participation by all stakeholders and communities. We would like to know how we can work together to implement decarbonization activities at a scale and in the pathways that interest you and members of your community. Please continue to be engaged and participate in RDF implementation.
Representation Terminology
We are sensitive to the concerns raised regarding representation terminology and use of the term “disadvantaged community”. We agree that the region needs to come together on terms and definitions in order to meet our goals of inclusivity and justice, and we would like to invite you to a regional discussion on this nomenclature. We have had many internal discussions of this topic so far, and the various terms that are used across agencies and agree conversations must continue. This is an important topic that needs consultation with frontline communities throughout San Diego county who would self-determine this regional approach. Our RDF technical study also shows that the integration of social equity in Climate Action Plans in the region is limited, inconsistent, and lacks specificity. We will have a preface statement clarifying the use of “disadvantaged community” in the Implementation Playbook that will recognize the need to have a regional conversation around representation terminology. We would welcome your input and comments on the development of guidance on terminology in the near future as part of an upcoming regional social equity working group that will be hosted by our Office.
We do however, want to note that with the intent to align regional climate-related activities across local jurisdictions, particularly to attract State and federal funds that are needed to support community-level involvement and work on future implementation projects, the term “disadvantaged community” is used consistently for both funding applications and processes. For example, the Justice40 Initiative in President Biden’s Executive Order 14008<https://www.whitehouse.gov/briefing-room/presidential-actions/2021/01/27/executive-order-on-tackling-the-climate-crisis-at-home-and-abroad/> (Section 223), State statutes such as Clean Energy and Pollution Act of 2015, and State laws for greenhouse gas reduction funds. We hope that we can continue to work together to ensure our frontline communities benefit from these investments in the future.
Stakeholder Inclusivity:
We recognize that improvements can always be made to be inclusive, and we welcome your thoughts on what actions could be taken, from a contracting standpoint or otherwise, to be more inclusive and better serve the community. Our County is committed to working with the community to co-create transformative, enduring structural, and systematic change in San Diego County government. We appreciate your attention to this and look forward to working with NAACP NSDC to refining our approach to date, to include groups that have not been reached by our efforts so far. Working together, we can build upon what we’ve been able to achieve, for example, through the Partners for Places grant. This grant supports BIPOC-led frontline organizations such as the Partnership for Advancement of New Americans, Majdal Center, YouthWill and the Global Action Research Center. Their reach is regional in nature, so that it covers District 3 as well as other districts. In addition, our Office recently co-partnered in a National Institute for Health grant application with UCSD School of Public Health and the Multicultural Health Foundation that serves mostly African Americans in Southeast San Diego. Although this grant application was not successful, we will continue to look for opportunities to fund similar partnerships with frontline communities. Our contractors on community engagement for the RDF regional convenings, Climate Action Campaign and The Urban Collaborative Project, were selected through a competitive solicitation process with criteria that emphasized community engagement of all the different demographics within each district. They have therefore put together a network of different community-based organizations to reach the unique communities of each district. This is just the starting point of what we can do as a region, and we welcome your input in this area.
Our community engagement to date, over a two-year period covering different stages of RDF studies, has included 32 public meetings with over 2,000 participants. In case anyone missed the meetings, they are posted on our website<https://www.sandiegocounty.gov/content/sdc/sustainability/regional-decarbonization/outreach-and-engagement.html> and we welcome participation through our Engage website<https://engage.sandiegocounty.gov/rdf>. We have had over 200 meetings with business, labor, community, environmental advocates, cities, tribes, regional agencies, etc. since our goal is to tailor the conversation to each group and meet them where they are. We will continue to reach out with more individuals and groups that have not yet been engaged in developing implementation options for this visionary framework.
We would like to work with NAACP NSDC to help us identify the organizations and community members for involvement and explore potential forms of partnership to help us reach zero carbon emissions in the region, together.
In closing, we appreciate the interest of NAACP NSDC executive leadership in participating in the RDF. We hope we have addressed your comments regarding the RDF timeline, representation terminology, and stakeholder inclusivity. We look forward to ongoing collaboration to strengthen all we have done to this point to engage the community, please feel free to reach me directly if you have any follow up questions or would like to set up a meeting.
Thank you,
Murtaza

Subject: [External] Response to Concerns (County RDF): NAACP North San Diego County

Greetings Chairwoman Vargas, Vice-Chair Lawson-Remer, and Board of Supervisors;

Please find attached a letter from the NAACP North San Diego County of significant issues that exist/ed in the County's Regional Decarbonization Framework. I will share some details of the sequence of events that prompted this letter with issues to be addressed. In general, we want to applaud the County for taking bold steps to address the climate crisis and environmental injustices. There are a lot of great things listed in the RDF. We also appreciate that the County is actively addressing the issues listed in the attached letter. As a public government body, it's important that these sequences of events are on record and noted to be addressed. This in itself helps to increase constituents' faith in our public officials. I want to say thank you, and we appreciate that our voices are being heard.

Public Sign of Bravery
I would like to share that many throughout the County felt it was commendable for Vice-Chair Lawson-Remer to stand with the janitorial union members on January 23, 2023, yet felt like the constituents in County District 3 were penalized for the RDF rescheduling when the public comments closed on February 2, 2023. As a member of our great County, I did address the RDF program management about this immediately.

Highlighted Issues
This letter highlights the inequitable process of the RDF project timeline, as well as other inequities to address that includes the following;

Extend the public comments section for the draft Implementation Playbook phase of the RDF to accommodate County District 3 constituents and residents.

Replace the terminology of "disadvantaged communities" that is meant to address the Black, Indigenous, People of Color communities with language that is acceptable from that community.

Adopt equitable contracting practice with Black frontline organizations throughout the RDF process. Include frontline communities as major stakeholders throughout the process.

Sequence of Events (How Did We Get Here)
I would like to share a brief list of sequence of events on the need to address the observation of inequities in the process of the County's Regional Decarbonization Framework.

Wednesday, February 1, 2023: I emailed Murtaza Baxamusa asking if the public comments were going to be extended until County District 3 has their convening.

As a member of the project team, this letter was emailed to Dr. Wooten and her team on Monday, February 13, 2023.

February 14, 2023, I had a discussion with Chairwoman Vargas senior staff, David Flores and he shared that Chairwoman Vargas agrees with the issues that are raised in this letter and that these matters are being addressed.

February 15, 2023, I had a discussion with Vice-chair Lawson-Remer’s staff, Rebecca Smith and she shared similar sentiments from my conversation with Chairwomen Vargas’s office. We also discussed perception from the public’s perspective of the timeline and public engagement in the process. She offered an open communication with Vice-chair Lawson-Remer’s office in sharing information that could be helpful from the community. Also, that the public feels like the March 15, 2023 Board vote is rushed.

This letter is being sent by the NAACP North San Diego County Branch. Many organizations, individuals, and groups share and support the positions listed in the letter. An example of some of the support includes:

Affinity clubs/groups, ADEMS, CEC, Women led workspace organizations, community based health professions, community members, environmental justice coalitions, Indivisible Groups, SURJ, Clean Earth 4Kids, San Diego Urban Sustainability Coalition, Interfaith Collaborations, Faith churches (North County, and the City of San Diego), Youth Focus Organizations, list of previous candidates for public office, etc.

Please feel free to contact us with any inquiries, comments, and questions.

Best regards and Environmentally yours,
Sonja Robinson
Chair, Environmental and Climate Justice Committee
NAACP North San Diego County

Dear UCSD team,

There is a departmental sustainability planning effort underway at the County that is quite unique, in that the plans were built up from the bottom-up by the staff working on the activities within the departments themselves rather than a high-level plan that may have difficulty getting actually implemented. Another unique feature of this effort is that there is a countywide steering committee with County staff that spans all the four functional groups covering all departments, so that there is coordination at the highest levels.

This departmental sustainability effort was directed by the Board last May, and the countywide sustainability goals were adopted in March this year; so the work (with Arup as consultant) has been proceeding somewhat on parallel track with the RDF.

Nicole from our office is leading this effort, and I wanted you all to be acquainted with it (see her email below) since it may come up in our meetings on RDF implementation and USP workshops. If you would like we can set up a meeting with Nicole.

Please let me know if you need any other background on this,
Murtaza

subject: List of Equity Impact Grant Winners - Cohort #1
body:
From:                                                       Leroy, Chiara
Sent:                                                         Friday, October 25, 2024 8:57 AM
To:                                                            Barbara Orozco-Valdivia
Subject:                                                   List of Equity Impact Grant Winners - Cohort #1

Good morning Barbara,

It was so nice spending time with you on Wednesday, catching up and talking shop. As promised, here
is the list of Equity Impact Grant winners for cohort #1. The cohort #2 winners should be announced
next week or so.
Building Justice (HoMEwork) – A Southeast San Diego organization that supports people
transitioning out of incarceration by prioritizing their personal development, creating a support
system, and providing opportunities to amplify their voices and inﬂuence policy decisions.
First Gen Scholars – An organization helping ﬁrst-generation, low-income Black, Latinx, and
Southeast Asian students navigate the college admissions process and graduate debt-free.
Free Thought Revolution – A community-driven eﬀort to “bridge the divide of humanity
through storytelling, community, and social action.” In addition to their podcast, their vision
includes educational initiatives and housing programs to provide a safe space for marginalized
individuals to engage in healing and community-building.
Garden 31 – This organization trains and mentors youth and adults that are considered at-risk,
formerly incarcerated, justice-impacted, and socioeconomically disadvantaged in regenerative
agriculture, sustainable food systems, and life skills to improve community health and wellness.
Inner-Tribal Treatment – To address the needs of the Native American population impacted by
the opioid crisis, this organization provides one of the only culturally-based treatment
programs in Southern California.
Lived Experiences – A North County community-based organization that utilizes data-proven
methods to advocate for change by investing in people’s microsystems and addressing the root
causes of physical and emotional trauma.
Majdal Arab Community Center of San Diego – Through advocacy and cultural programs, this
East County organization works to empower and uplift the Arab community in San Diego.
Paddle for Peace – An organization conceived to create a nurturing space where BIPOC children
could not only access coastal environments for recreation, physical ﬁtness and mental healing
but also envision and explore careers in Marine Biology and Environmentalism. To date, they
have provided over 600 ﬁrst time coastal experiences for BIPOC, underserved youth.
San Diego Community Birth Center – This is the only Black-owned birth center in San Diego
County, providing access to midwifery care, doula and lactation services, among other
resources that ensure healthy births.
San Diego Black LGBTQ Coalition – A volunteer-led organization that not only serves over 500
Black LGBTQ people and families yearly but works to address the acute needs of the Black
transgender community.

Sharing some additional resources that may be of use:
Community Leadership Teams, including links to each region’s website (which has each region’s
priority areas listed), and the 2008-2025 Community Health Assessments
Equity Impact Report, provides “baseline synopsis of the impact of systemic racial inequities
throughout our County”

Please let me know if there’s anything else that I can share with you.
Talk soon and good luck canvassing!

Warmly,

Chiara

Since Max will already be in attendance he will be available to be the point person on this.

The County is currently evaluating the feasibility of storm drain diversions to water recycling facilities. As such, we are looking to map (via GIS data) local sewer networks and sewersheds draining to water recycling facilities (both direct potable reuse and recycled water [“purple pipe”]). We are also interested in mapping the service areas for all local direct potable reuse facilities, water recycling facilities, and desalination facilities. It would be very helpful if each representative could provide a publicly available data source or identify a subject matter expert (and provide contact information) for more information on obtaining this data.

We will most likely also need to reach out to specific water districts/agencies, but this could be a very helpful start!

To: Brukman, Eden <Eden.Brukman@sdcounty.ca.gov>
Cc: Murphy, Meghan <Meghan.Murphy@sdcounty.ca.gov>; Freeman, Rhonda <Rhonda.Freeman@sdcounty.ca.gov>; Wooten, Wilma <Wilma.Wooten@sdcounty.ca.gov>
Subject: Invitation to Food Services Leadership Committee Meeting on September 20th re. County Food Procurement Policy

Good Morning Eden,

I wanted to introduce myself.  My name is Elizabeth Hernandez, and I am the Director of Public Health Services (PHS).  On behalf of PHS, I’m writing to let you know about an ARPA funded program we lead that has some relevant touch points with your office and to invite you to an upcoming meeting.

The Sustainable, Equitable, and Local Food Sourcing Program and Policy focuses on County food procurement to direct public dollars through food purchasing towards value categories that reflect broader County of San Diego goals. Specifically, the Program and Policy prioritize Board directed value categories to ensure that County of San Diego food service operation purchases positively impact a sustainable, equitable, and local food system. Values-based food sourcing prioritizes principles that go beyond just price when deciding which food items to purchase. The values include: local sourcing, equity-informed sourcing, elevated labor standards, organic or regenerative certification, low-carbon intensity, and nutritional co-benefit. As you can see, there are several value categories that overlap with the Office of Sustainability and Environmental Justice.

We have contracted with nationally recognized organizations in the field of values-based food procurement (Karen Karp & Partners and the Center for Good Food Purchasing) to provide technical assistance to our County’s food service operations and program managers. We are wrapping up our first year of implementation of the program which has included assessing purchasing data and collaboratively developing action plans. Our team is also working on developing a policy for the Sustainable, Equitable, and Local Food Sourcing Program with a return to the Board date of 12/5. This will include an Environmental and Economic Assessment.

We would like to invite you to the next Food Services Leadership Committee meeting on September 20th, where the TA providers will provide an overview of program progress so far. We’ll also have time set aside during the meeting to receive input and review from the food service operators and program leads on the draft policy. The Food Services Leadership Committee is made up of all County of San Diego food service operations and is also attended by Rebeca Appel, who is a part of the Office of Sustainability and Environmental Justice.

I’m attaching relevant Board Letters to this email for additional context. Before the September 20th meeting, you will be hearing from our Project Lead, Meghan Murphy (copied), who will schedule a time to further brief you on the Program and Policy as well as answer any questions you may have.  We are looking forward to connecting with you on this exciting program!

Thank you,

Elizabeth A. Hernandez, Ph.D.

Director

Public Health Services
County of San Diego Health & Human Services Agency

	Cc: Lauren Serrano <lserrano@ucsd.edu <mailto:lserrano@ucsd.edu> >; jhinds@ucsd.edu <mailto:jhinds@ucsd.edu> ; gmccord@ucsd.edu <mailto:gmccord@ucsd.edu> ; nschieff@ucsd.edu <mailto:nschieff@ucsd.edu>
	Subject: Re: [External] Re: Invitation: County Workshop #2 Planning Meeting @ Fri Jan 20, 2023 9am - 10am (PST) (amlerner@ucsd.edu <mailto:amlerner@ucsd.edu> )

	Hi Murtaza,

	Here is what we have so far:

	The Regional Development Framework for San Diego County provides pathways for getting to zero emissions in the county, including energy generation, transportation, natural climate solutions, and buildings. Decarbonization of buildings is especially important because the County and local jurisdictions must work together to provide similar incentives and building codes for consistency across the San Diego region. Workshop 2 will bring together key staff and leadership in the incorporated cities, County, and key external stakeholders to: (1) develop a common understanding of the RDF’s building decarbonization goals and strategies; (2) outline roles of local ordinances, state codes, and utility policies in decarbonization actions; and (3) build consensus on common, cross-jurisdiction strategies as well as individual approaches.  Participants also will be asked to identify where state legislation, investment, or regulatory change is needed to support building decarbonization.

	Prior to the workshop, UCSD will prepare summaries of existing building energy regulations and incentives in each of San Diego County’s 16 jurisdictions, establishing a framework for identifying commonalities, differences, and options among and across jurisdictions.  Existing and planned utility programs and incentives also will be compiled so participants can see where and how these support or conflict with local needs.  Case studies with cost information (where applicable) will be identified for presentation during the workshop to highlight how decarbonization takes place in practice.

	Let us know what you think.

Subject: [External] Invitation to join new Ag Workforce Initiative in San Diego

Hi Murtaza and Rebeca,

It was great to see you both at the D4 RDF convening this week! It was great timing to be hearing about the workforce components in particular, as we are hosting a series of Ag Workforce meetings in partnership with Foodshed.

We would love to invite you both to participate in this Agricultural Workforce Initiative in San Diego County. Led by Foodshed Small Farm Distro and funded by a CDFA Workforce Development Grant, this new initiative aims to support farmer-led training and workforce development in the region.

Over the next few months we will be facilitating a series of small group meetings to inform the development of a Workforce Development Needs Assessment, strengthen relationships among beginning farmer training programs, and guide future workforce development programs.

[cid:185e0ed24014cff311]

Please let me know if you are able to attend. Don't hesitate to reach out with any questions, we hope to have you join these important discussions!

Warmly,
Rachel & Sona

Subject: [External] RE: RWER Requested Scope Amendments

Hi Stephanie,

I hope you had a nice weekend.

I understand this is coming in late after having already discussed and submitted the proposed amendment, but I wanted to see if there might still be a possibility of adding slightly more budget for Task 6 to address the equity components/analyses. We would like to prepare some region-wide maps, setting the current condition of a few select equity metrics (e.g., affordable, safe, etc.) and then applying similar criteria to the potential enhancements. In doing the final projected staff forecasting late last week, I found we are a little short on budget to carry this forward, primarily because the original TO was framed as the "Drought Assessment" rather than the "Regional Water Equity Report," so these equity-based analyses were not anticipated.

Let me know what you think or if you would like to discuss this over the phone.

Thanks,

Megan

The last few years have demonstrated the impact of drought and the changing magnitude and frequency of our precipitation events. Now, more than ever, the work in the stormwater management field is critical to achieving a more resilient future. Collectively, our actions can lead to a Rain Ready California. What does that look like? Investing in our communities to reconnect the hydrologic cycle (e.g., stormwater capture). Rethinking how we work to integrate across water sectors to achieve our shared common goals. Protecting our waterways through true source control and effective BMPs. Engaging within the stormwater profession and the communities we serve to communicate that stormwater is a resource. Advocating for funding, regulations, and legislation to support these outcomes. And most importantly, learning from each other to make it all possible.

Max Dugan, PE
Senior Engineer

Hi Stephanie,

I hope you had a nice weekend.

I understand this is coming in late after having already discussed and submitted the proposed amendment, but I wanted to see if there might still be a possibility of adding slightly more budget for Task 6 to address the mapping components/analyses. We would like to prepare some watershed-wide maps showing the current condition of the private structural BMP inventory (e.g., BMP type, maintenance status, etc.) and then applying similar criteria to the proposed inspection prioritization. In doing the final projected staff forecasting late last week, I found we are a little short on budget to carry this forward, primarily because the original TO was framed as the “Inventory Update” rather than the “Program Assessment,” so these mapping analyses were not anticipated.

Let me know what you think or if you would like to discuss this over the phone. I know this week is mostly RWER review for you, so whenever works.

Subject: RE: Onsite Treatment and Reuse of Non-potable Water

Hi Stephanie,

Below are my notes on the proposed regulations for Onsite Treatment and Reuse of Non-potable Water.

Regulatory Objective

To establish risk-based log reduction targets for the removal of pathogens such as enteric viruses, parasitic protozoa, and enteric bacteria for non-potable water sources (graywater, rainwater, stormwater, and blackwater), and non-potable end uses (toilet and urinal flushing, clothes washing, irrigation, and dust suppression).

Non-potable water sources

Non-potable end uses

*	Graywater
*	Rainwater
*	Stormwater
*	Blackwater

*	Toilet Flushing
*	Clothes Washing
*	Irrigation
*	Dust Suppression

Exclusions

Regulations do not apply to:

*	Untreated graywater systems that are used exclusively for subsurface irrigation
*	Untreated rainwater systems that are used exclusively for surface, subsurface, or drip irrigation
*	Municipal stormwater capture and use systems

What systems are subject to the new regulations?

An onsite treatment system is subject to the new regulations if:

*	It treats one or more of the following water sources, in whole or in part:

	*	Rainwater
	*	Stormwater
	*	Graywater, or
	*	Blackwater

*	The water sources are collected, treated, and used onsite
*	The treated water is used for non-potable purpose
*	It is connected to community sewer system as its only mean for disposal (blackwater system)

The regulations are intended for building-scale or district-scale (multiple buildings or campus) systems onsite reuse.

Risk-based Water Quality Standard

The goal is to achieve a (microbial) risk level of health protection from pathogens in onsite treated water of 1 in 10,000 infections per person per year. This is consistent with acceptable risk for EPA drinking water regulations and State of CA potable reuse regulations.

There will be two sets of log reduction targets for 1) indoor uses (toilet flushing, clothes washing) and 2) outdoor uses (irrigation, dust control, fire suppression, and car washing).

Schedule

The State Water Board is required to adopt the regulations by December 1, 2022. The Department of Housing and Community Development is required to develop and propose for adoption any necessary corresponding building standards to support the regulations adopted by the State Water Board by December 1, 2023.

The State Water Board’s website <https://www.waterboards.ca.gov/drinking_water/certlic/drinkingwater/onsite_nonpotable_reuse_regulations.html>  for the program offers no evidence that the regulation have been finalized. All procedural dates are listed as TBD.

Let me know if you have any questions you’d like me to look into.

Thanks,

Chris

Subject: [External] Onsite Treatment and Reuse of Non-potable Water

Kacen, Stephanie,

Here is some follow-up information from the Policy and Permitting Subcommittee call. The Division of Drinking Water is developing regulations for the Onsite Treatment and Reuse of Non-potable Water. This is a legislative mandate. California Water Code section 13558 requires the State Water Board to adopt regulations on or before December 1, 2022. I just checked the website, and the schedule is still listed as TBD.

There was a workshop earlier this year and several stormwater representatives participated asking a lot of questions about whether this will affect our capture and use projects. The outcome was including the following statement in the FAQ, which is somewhat reassuring, however this might be something to track as the underlying language in the legislation and the draft information shared remains confusing.

12. Will the proposed regulations apply to municipal stormwater capture and use systems? No. The regulations are intended for building-scale or district-scale (multiple buildings or campus) systems onsite reuse. Watershed-scale stormwater capture projects designed to collect and store watershed-wide runoff during dry or wet weather conditions would not fit into the definition of OTNWS since the collection of the source water (stormwater) and in many cases, the use, are not onsite.

See more info here:  https://www.waterboards.ca.gov/drinking_water/certlic/drinkingwater/onsite_nonpotable_reuse_regulations.html <https://www.waterboards.ca.gov/drinking_water/certlic/drinkingwater/onsite_nonpotable_reuse_regulations.html>

subject: [External] Presenting at our Fallbrook Climate Action Team Meeting
body:
Dr Elise
I heard you speak at the San Diego County heat and health community meeting on Jan 31, 2023.
We give monthly 1 hour presentations related to Climate Change to people interested in learning about
Climate Change.  Our audience can  be professors, doctors, average citizens, people working for
climate change related companies and local politicians.

Would you be interested in doing a presentation for us on what you covered?

The presentations are usually 45-50 minutes via Zoom with 10-15 minutes for questions.

Also I understand the only version of the RDF is a draft copy.  Is that something you would also like to talk about?

Look forward to hearing from you.
Regards
Deanna Parks
Fallbrook Climate Action Team
760-803-6934
rationale: Criteria (3)/(4): a June 2023 email to Elise Ruiz whose only hit is the aside that the RDF is still a draft; the main request is a talk based on a heat and health meeting.

subject: RE: [External] Re: Extreme Heat Survey Questions
body:
Good afternoon Ali,

Thanks so much for reaching out about the August 28th presentation, we are looking forward to this opportunity! The presentation usually takes about 10 minutes, and can be shortened if needed. We are still in the process of determining who would present from our team, and I will make sure to get you their info and bio once confirmed.

A few other follow up items:

*	I’ve attached the blurb we would like to include for the newsletter, please feel free to let me know if the wording should be adjusted or if you have recommendations of how previous RDF newsletters may have been drafted.

As for the survey questions below, sorry if I overlooked this in previous emails, but yes absolutely please feel free to add modifications to the heat question as we discussed during our meeting.

Thanks so much!

Elise

Hi Elise,

Just checking in on our inquiry below regarding Northern Baja regions to focus on?

Also, please see attached for a revised Stakeholder Interview List that has three phases described below.  I’d like to provide a short summary of our thinking behind this.  The building/cooling focus interviews are more technical in nature, so we feel like we can get those going sooner than later.  For the Task 2A longer list of stakeholders (15 to be interviewed), we didn’t want to start with too many as there are some decisions that still need to be made regarding the 15 to be interviewed.  Therefore, we only proposed 4 stakeholders on this list where we feel they would provide good input and would take less strategy to establish the interviews.  Most agricultural stakeholders are split between Phase 2 and Phase 3, we think the Phase 2 list could likely be reviewed by your team fairly quickly and would take less messaging strategy (e.g. for the national agriculture stakeholders that were proposed by re-focus).  We anticipate that the local agricultural stakeholders will take more strategy and are therefore listed under Phase 3.

  1.  Phase 1 – these stakeholders would require less strategy on messaging during the interview where our team/subs could be ready for interview scheduling now.
  2.  Phase 2 – these stakeholders require some strategy, and a meeting between our team/County is necessary to finalize messaging.
  3.  Phase 3 – these stakeholders require a lot of coordination between our team/County and require strategic messaging during the interviews.

Let’s plan to discuss this at our standing meeting on Wednesday and any questions you may have.  If possible, I think a good goal would be to get some of these Phase 1 stakeholder interviews going in a week from now to stay on schedule.  I’ll also plan to update the Sharepoint site with this revised matrix.

Thank you,
Stephanie

Subject: RE: Connect with OSEJ Team & Next Steps

Hello all,

Thank you for your time and for the thoughtful discussion yesterday! Our team really appreciated the opportunity to connect with you all.

As I mentioned during the meeting, I am happy to meet and discuss the Resilience Hubs effort in more detail. I have attached the Project Fact Sheet and the flyer for the virtual Deep Dive events to share with your communities, and we have these documents translated in the threshold languages, which I can send to you separately.

The Deep Dive series is scheduled through the beginning of September, and we appreciate you sharing the flyer with your networks to inform communities about these events, as their feedback is greatly valued on this topic. You can also refer to the OSEJ website <https://www.sandiegocounty.gov/osej/>  to stay informed on upcoming events and project updates. We will continue to stay connected with you and please feel free to let us know if you have any questions.

Have a great evening!

Elise

Subject: Climate Action Research Grant - Letter of Intent (LOI) Due Jan 17th

Hi Everyone:

I hope you are all doing well and had a wonderful holiday season!  I am writing to provide an overview of the Climate Action Research Grant Program and the formation of a San Diego based team, and next steps.

Climate Action Research Grant Program

Just before the holidays in December, the state of California finally released the long awaited call for research (and action) proposals for projects that can demonstrate the ability to hit the ground running and sustain lasting practical and GHG mitigation, reduction and  impacts.  These will be 2 year projects ranging from around 500k up to $10 Million.  A letter of intent (LOI)  is due January 17th which is very soon for projects both with or without matching funds.

We are fortunate to have received a great deal of enthusiasm from all of the partners needed to generate a very competitive application.  The City of San Diego, San Diego County, SANDAG, the Climate Action Campaign, UCSD and other research partners have the ability to form a very strong team with complementary roles and skills that meet the requirements of this RFP.  Each organization has expressed an interest in working together to leverage our collective strengths, expertise, resources, and interests to create a strong and competitive LOI.  It is also possible that we may have the ability to show a significant matching funds by directly supporting other synergistic efforts underway in our region.  Foremost, I will soon be introducing the researchers who will be part of this effort – drawn from several research institutions.

We all share a collective interest and vision for reducing travel and place-based GHG emissions, providing affordable housing, and promoting public health, social justice, and safety through transit and active transportation investments combined with sustainable land use practices.  The policy and regulatory environment is rapidly changing with significant advancements at the state, regional, and local level taking place.  The immediate goal is to craft a compelling LOI that is sufficiently focused and targeted while also being general enough to be something we can all agree to quickly to get the green light from the state to move on to the proposal development stage where we will truly craft our work plan and what we want to accomplish.  There is a tremendous amount of work underway within each of our member organizations to generate a very unique and compelling project.

Next Steps

1.  Confirming who is on our team
2.  Getting your input - convening to discuss focus for LOI – stay tuned
3.  Drafting the AIMS, objectives, approach, and products
4.  Creating budget, timeline, and confirming match
5.  Completing letters of support
6.  Meeting all LOI requirements (see below)
7.  Filing LOI by the 17th
RFP Overview
The RFP can be found at this link: 2023 Request for Proposals (RFP) for the California Climate Action Research Initiative.  “The CA Climate Action Research Grants are intended to spur innovative applied research that addresses California’s climate goals, ensures that local communities are prepared and resilient, and prevents future disasters. This Request for Proposals (RFP) outlines two grant categories: CA Climate Action Seed Grants and CA Climate Action Matching Grants. Proposals for both grant categories must be synergistic with the State of California’s climate action priority or priorities. The California Climate Adaptation Strategy, in particular, presents a holistic vision for the state with the following outcome- based priorities:
1.  Strengthen protections for climate vulnerable communities
2.  Bolster public health and safety to protect against increasing climate risks
3.  Build a climate resilient economy
4.  Accelerate nature-based climate solutions and strengthen climate resilience of natural systems
5.  Make decisions based on the best available climate science
6.  Partner and collaborate to leverage resources
There are several goals and actions under each priority area. Together, this set of priorities requires the participation of multiple disciplines and different types of partners. There are also many other state resources and strategic plans that highlight agency-specific priorities. Appendix A provides a partial list of these resources.  An important emphasis of both grant programs is near-term outcome-based solutions for public impact. (See Sec. 2.4.) To that end, proposal teams must consider thoughtful partnerships, broadly defined based on the proposed project, that will lead to high-impact solutions informed by collective insights and experiences.
Letter of Intent
A letter of intent (LOI) is required for both grant categories. The Applicant PI must specify whether they are applying for a Seed Grant or Matching Grant. Then they must complete the appropriate application materials in the RGPO SmartSimple portal.
Letter of Intent Content. LOI submissions must include the following information:
*   Proposal title (100 characters or less)
*   Identification of Applicant PI and three-page biosketch/CV upload
*   Identification of Co-PIs, Co-Investigators/senior personnel, and other participating personnel
and/or organizations, institutions, or agencies, and a three-page biosketch/CV for each
o IdentifyatleastoneotherCaliforniaacademic/researchinstitutioncollaborator(requiredfor
Matching Grant; encouraged for Seed Grant).
o Identify at least one community/end-user partner (required for Matching Grant; encouraged for
Seed Grant). See Appendix B.
*   Specific California climate priority or priorities the research will address, with links to supporting
agency documents or reports (required). See Appendix A.
*   Actionable outcome(s) expected from the project
*   Abstract/Project Summary addressing the proposed scope of research and activities, rationale, and
potential impact and expected outcomes (2400 characters max)
*   Brief plans for required programmatic components, including collaboration plan, plan for engaging
communities and other end-users, and approach to leveraging available climate related resources,
or infrastructure.
*   Keywords: Research Categories and Identifiers to be selected from a drop-down menu.
*   Seed Grants only: Specific plan for leveraging the Seed Grant during or immediately after grant
period (specific grant or other funding source or opportunity)
*   Matching Grants only: Anticipated contributions for matching commitments (cash and/or in-kind).
See Appendix C.

Subject: Announcement: Welcome Bethany Facendini, OSEJ GPM Community Engagement

Greetings All,

I am thrilled to introduce Bethany Facendini, our new Community Engagement and Outreach Manager for the Office of Sustainability and Environmental Justice (OSEJ). Bethany is an experienced community organizer and sustainability advocate, and she will lead our efforts to engage and empower diverse communities throughout our region for climate action.

Bethany will develop and implement strategies to foster community connections and participation in environmental justice and sustainability initiatives. She will work closely with community benefit organizations, leaders, practitioners, and residents to create opportunities for collaboration and partnership.

Bethany brings a wealth of experience and expertise to OSEJ, including numerous community engagement roles in the San Francisco Bay Area and beyond, most recently with Sonoma County Regional Parks as the Community Engagement Division Manager. There, she directed marketing, communications, and cross-sector partnerships, as well as created sustainability and equity-based programs for diverse audiences, community needs assessments, and evaluation systems. In addition, Bethany helped increase the number of culturally relevant programs for under-represented populations (BIPOC, youth impacted by systems, people with disabilities, and families with low incomes). She also served as Sonoma County Human Services’ Community Engagement Manager where she led community programs to increase awareness of services and community outreach events; cultivated relationships between private, governmental, and non-profit organizations to improve partnerships; and built community networks to connect marginalized groups to programs and services. From 2013 – 2015 as the Community Engagement Coordinator for the Sonoma County Department of Health Services, Bethany worked on community engagement and outreach to advance health equity systems change initiatives. She has a Master of Arts in Environmental and Social Justice and a Bachelor of Arts degree in English and LGBTQ Studies. She also has an Urban Environmental Education Certification from Cornell University.

Bethany has world travel and living abroad experience in 46 countries, mostly economically developing nations, and recently returned from a year-long sabbatical traveling solo around the world.

We are excited to have Bethany on board and look forward to her leadership in advancing our environmental justice and sustainability goals. Please join me in welcoming Bethany to our team.

Enjoy the day,

eden

Eden Brukman, Chief Sustainability Officer

Subject: RE: CBO Regional Water Equity - Water Questions

Fantastic! In general, the questions look fine. A couple observations (take or leave as y'all see fit to gather the information you need):

*	Q2. Is there value to asking this as a question at the personal level or offer it as "you and your community" to encourage them to speak about what they know?
*	Q2 and Q3 are both framed as concerns/challenges; is there a question that can be asked that is situational or neutral in its implications to help balance the inquiry? How do you use water? What strategies have you observed or used to support water conservation? Or something along those lines for context...
*	It might be useful to have a general field for other comments they may want to share about water that doesn't fit into the formal responses.
*	(I imagine that CAC is requesting zip code or similar geolocator.)
